records.title: Association between Brain Amyloid Status and Cognitive and Physical Performance in Older Adults with Frailty Criteria: Longitudinal Data from the CogFrail Study
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: The impact of cerebral amyloid pathology on cognitive and functional decline may differ with age. Evidence linking brain amyloidopathy to physical decline remains limited and inconsistent. This study investigated the association between brain amyloid status and cognitive and physical decline in (pre)frail older adults with cognitive impairment.  This longitudinal analysis used data from the CogFrail study. Brain amyloid pathology was assessed using amyloid-positron emission tomography (visual reading). Linear mixed-effects models examined differences over a two-year follow-up between amyloid-positive and amyloid-negative participants in cognitive, functional, and physical trajectories. Cognitive and functional outcomes included the Mini-Mental State Examination, the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes, the Activities of Daily Living Index, and a neuropsychological battery, while the physical domain was assessed using handgrip strength, chair rise time, gait speed, and the Short Physical Performance Battery.  Among 199 participants (mean age 82.3 ± 4.8 years; 65.3% women), 108(54.3%) were amyloid-positive. Amyloid-positive participants experienced greater decline in the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes (β = 0.30, 95% CI 0.10–0.49; p = 0.003, log-transformed) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (β = –1.62, 95% CI –2.74 to –0.49; p = 0.005). No significant longitudinal differences were observed between groups in the Activities of Daily Living Index, neuropsychological outcomes, or physical performance measures.  Amyloid pathology assessment may help differentiate cognitive trajectories in cognitively impaired (pre)frail older adults. Greater cognitive decline in amyloid-positive participants was not associated with greater loss of independence or additional physical decline over time. TRIAL REGISTRATION NCT03129269

records.title: Older Adults Seeking Publicly Funded Long-Term Care in a Super-ageing Society: Trends in Functional Impairments and Multimorbidity Burden Based on InterRAI-Home Care Data From 2001 to 2019 in Hong Kong
records.abstract: Understanding changes in long-term care (LTC) applicants’ needs informs service planning.  To examine trends in functional impairment and multimorbidity among Hong Kong’s publicly funded LTC applicants during 2001–2019.  We analyzed interRAI assessments from 315,556 applicants aged ≥60. Hierarchical mixed-effects models estimated trends in physical and cognitive impairment, loneliness, and multimorbidity, adjusting for age, birth cohort, and sociodemographic factors. Subgroup analyses examined differences by age, disease, and living status.  Cognitive impairment and multimorbidity increased, physical impairment plateaued, and loneliness declined. Stroke was associated with greater physical and cognitive impairment, and cataract with greater loneliness. Applicants aged ≥85 had more functional impairments but less multimorbidity.  Applicants’ functional and health needs became more complex and varied over time, differing by age, living arrangements, and disease profiles. These findings support integrated, tailored strategies to address changing health and social needs of older adults applying for publicly funded LTC services.

records.title: Neighborhood Characteristics, Behavioral Symptoms of Cognitive Decline, and Caregivers’ Distress in Older Mexican Americans
records.abstract: We use person-environment (PE) fit theory to examine whether neighborhood composition is associated with behavioral symptoms of cognitive decline among older Mexican Americans and their caregivers’ distress.  We estimated multilevel regression models using 2011/2012 data from the Hispanic Established Population for the Epidemiological Study of the Elderly ( n = 862) linked to 2010 census tract characteristics (percent foreign born, Hispanic, and poor) from the National Neighborhood Data Archive, adjusting for care recipient and caregiver covariates.  Residing in areas with a higher proportion of foreign-born adults was associated with fewer neuropsychiatric symptoms, particularly delusions, agitation/aggression, depression/dysphoria, and anxiety, and with lower symptom severity. Higher tract poverty was marginally associated with greater odds of aberrant motor behavior, while tract characteristics were unrelated to caregiver distress. Discussion Findings support a PE-fit interpretation in which immigrant enclaves, rather than Hispanic concentration, may influence behavioral symptom expression or their perceptions/reporting by caregivers.

records.title: Depressive Symptoms as Mediators of the Relationship Between Sensory Impairment and Cognitive Function in Community-Dwelling Older Couples: An Actor–Partner Interdependence Mediation Model
records.abstract: This study examined the indirect associations between sensory impairment and cognitive function through depressive symptoms using the Actor–Partner Interdependence Mediation Model (APIMeM).  We analyzed dyadic data from 2,233 older adult couples. The outcome variable was cognitive function, while the independent variables were sensory impairments. Depressive symptoms were examined as the mediator. We utilized the APIMeM to examine within-person and cross-partner indirect associations through depressive symptoms.  Significant actor–actor indirect associations were observed for males and females in all three models, together with several cross-partner indirect associations. Dual sensory and hearing findings were generally maintained in sensitivity analyses. For vision impairment, actor–actor associations remained robust, whereas two smaller cross-partner associations were attenuated in the expanded sample.  Depressive symptoms were associated with within-person and cross-partner relationships between sensory impairment and cognitive function. These findings highlight the importance of considering both spouses.

records.title: Pain and self-rated health in the very old: Individual participant data meta-analysis from five TULIP Consortium cohorts
records.abstract: In adults and older adults, pain is inversely associated with self-rated health (SRH) independent of health status. Less is known about this association in the very old. This paper aims to determine how pain is associated with SRH in very old people with and without adjustment for individual health status.  Using data from five cohorts of very old people aged 80+ from different cultural contexts (n=2,664), we separately fitted single- and multi-level logistic models of SRH to examine cross-sectional and longitudinal associations with pain, respectively. We performed random effects meta-analysis to combine cohort-specific odds ratios (ORs) of positive SRH (selecting response options ‘good’ and above) for those reporting any pain in the past month, at baseline and then over time for up to 10 years follow-up, with adjustment for sociodemographic (age, sex, income status) and individual health (multimorbidity, depressive symptoms, functional ability) variables.  Over half of participants across cohorts (55.4%) reported having pain and 71.1% had positive SRH at baseline. At baseline, the odds of positive SRH were significantly lower in those with pain in all cohorts when we adjusted for sociodemographic variables (combined OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.28, 0.48), which persisted when we added health-related variables to the models (combined OR 0.42; 95% CI 0.34, 0.54). In longitudinal analysis, over time pain remained significantly associated with lower odds of positive SRH throughout follow-up (combined OR 0.45; 95% CI 0.35, 0.58) after adjusting for sociodemographic and individual health variables.  Pain is common in very old people, and it is associated with worse SRH independent of health status at baseline and over time. This inverse association is consistent across cultures and time, highlighting the importance of addressing pain in this age group.

records.title: Differential care demands on Medicare patients by multimorbidity group: care continuity, care coordination, and contact days
records.abstract: Patients with multimorbidity face multiple care demands, including the time to access care and the cognitive effort of coordinating care. It is unclear how patients’ experiences with care continuity, coordination, and time burdens (i.e., health care contact days) vary across multimorbidity groups or what role potential protective factors may play.  This cross-sectional study used the nationally representative 2022 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey linked with traditional Medicare claims from the United States. We included continuously enrolled, community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 65 with ≥ 2 chronic conditions. We described self-reported experiences of care continuity and care coordination, health care contact days (receiving ambulatory or institutional care), and telehealth days, home visits, and remote monitoring by multimorbidity group (low: 2–3 chronic conditions, medium: 4–6, high: 7+).  Among 4424 respondents, care experiences varied by multimorbidity group. Adults in the high multimorbidity group often reported having a usual source of care (96.6%), one provider knowing all of their medical needs (84.4%), and their primary care physician (PCP) being informed about specialist care (81.3%). Fewer patients in the medium and high multimorbidity groups reported satisfaction with co-localized care and ease of managing care, while fewer patients in the low multimorbidity group reported satisfaction with specialist availability. Mean contact days ranged from 12.6 (SD 13.4) per year (low multimorbidity group) to 31.3 (SD 23.9) (high multimorbidity). More patients in the high multimorbidity group used telehealth, home care, and remote monitoring.  Care experiences vary across multimorbidity groups, with high-multimorbidity patients experiencing greater continuity but also greater difficulty managing care. The findings suggest a potential need to improve specialist access and informational continuity in the low multimorbidity group, support care management and co-localized care in the higher multimorbidity groups and reduce care complexity and potentially avoidable contact days across multimorbidity groups.

records.title: Translation, cultural adaptation and psychometric evaluation of the age-friendly cities and communities questionnaire for Sweden
records.abstract: The Age-Friendly Cities and Communities Questionnaire (AFCCQ) measures how older people perceive the age-friendliness of their city or community. With 23% of Swedish residents projected to be aged ≥ 65 years by 2040, a culturally adapted and psychometrically validated Swedish version (AFCCQ-SE) is needed to guide age-friendly initiatives nationally. This study aimed to translate the AFCCQ into Swedish and to conduct its cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric validation.  In Phase I, the AFCCQ-EN was independently forward-translated into Swedish and back-translated into English. Ten older adults and ten academic experts then rated each item’s relevance on a 4-point scale. In Phase II, 874 community-dwelling Swedes aged ≥ 65 years (64.9% female; mean age 75.7 ± 5.8 years; 82.8% urban) from two regions completed the AFCCQ-SE. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was used to assess the nine-domain structure against fit criteria and composite reliability (CR) was used to evaluate internal consistency. Rasch analysis examined various aspects of the AFCCQ at the item and rating scale level.  I-CVI values of all items ranged from 0.80 to 1.00 (mostly 0.90). CFA supported the proposed nine-domain structure (χ²[194] = 562.9; normed χ² = 2.90; CFI = 0.962; TLI = 0.951; SRMR = 0.0335; RMSEA = 0.047). CR values were acceptable across most domains (0.783–0.937), with two domains marginally below the threshold (0.658–0.699). Rasch analyses showed acceptable rating categories and satisfactory item fit. Urban–rural DIF was found for two transportation items (0.51 & 0.71 logits, Holm adjusted p = 0.000). PCA supported unidimensionality within each domain rather than for the questionnaire as a whole. Twenty-two item pairs showed local dependence ( r = 0.16–0.84), 21 of them within a single domain. Aggregating the items into nine testlets largely resolved local dependence (largest residual correlation = 0.10), and the first residual contrast eigenvalue decreased from 3.32 to 1.52 (  This AFCCQ-SE study, using both CFA and Rasch analysis, provided preliminary support for its psychometric properties in this Swedish sample. Further validation using samples from larger regions and longitudinal study designs is needed to verify these findings.

records.title: Co-Creating a Patient-Reported Outcome Measure for Social Robots in Dementia Care
records.abstract: Introduction Social robots (SRs) show promise in supporting persons living with dementia (PLWD). However, tools that measure their impact from the perspectives of the dementia community are lacking. This study describes the initial phase of a research program to co-create a Patient-Reported Outcome Measure (PROM) for the use of SRs in dementia care.  We conducted 10 co-creation workshops, five online and five in-person, with members of the dementia community (N=51; PLWD, care partners and healthcare providers), informed by a research advisory group (N=8).  Participants identified 47 candidate PROM items across eight domains: interactions, mental and emotional wellness, activities, caregiver experiences, health, safety and security, quality of life, and independence. Preferences for PROM administration include brief completion time, use of plain language and being available on paper and in digital format.  This study provides a conceptual foundation for the development of a PROM for use of SRs in dementia care. Findings highlight a broad range of potential outcomes and underscore the value of capturing user-centered perspectives in a systematic way. In the next phases of PROM development, we will develop a draft PROM before evaluating its measurement properties and testing it in real-world settings. This program of research aims to strengthen the evaluation of SRs by facilitating meaningful assessment of user experiences to generate insights that inform healthcare policy, technology development, and empower end-users to make informed decisions about using SRs in dementia care.

records.title: Associations Between Neighborhood Service, Religious, and Civic Organizations and Cognitive Decline for Older Mexican Americans Residing in Urban and Rural Areas
records.abstract: Neighborhood resources are protective factors for healthy cognitive aging, yet the impact of these resources may vary by urbanicity. We examined urban-rural differences in the association between the availability of neighborhood social services, religious, and civic organizations, and cognitive decline among older Mexican Americans. Method Data from 628 participants ( M Age = 80) in 2004–2013 Hispanic Established Populations for the Epidemiologic Study of the Elderly were linked to the National Neighborhood Data Archive. Cognitive impairment was measured with the Mini-Mental State Examination.  Among urban residents, the presence of religious organizations was associated with better cognition levels, but a higher number of civic organizations were linked to worse levels and a steeper decline in cognition. There were no effects of neighborhood resources on cognition among rural residents. Discussion The differential impacts of organization types and urbanicity should be considered when promoting cognitively protective neighborhood resources for older Mexican Americans.

records.title: Impact of Hearing and Vision Loss on Quality of Life in Older Adults Living With Cognitive Impairment: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: Previous reviews have established that hearing and vision impairments are common among people living with cognitive impairment and that these comorbidities can exacerbate effects of cognitive impairments on cognitive, social and functional outcomes. This scoping review aimed to extend on this knowledge, by identifying and evaluating evidence regarding the effect of hearing and vision impairment on quality of life among older adults living with cognitive impairment, to: (i) determine if a compounding effect exists between hearing and/or vision and cognitive impairments; (ii) compare the effects on hearing, vision and health-related quality of life, and (iii) evaluate quality of life outcomes for hearing and vision interventions for this population. Seven electronic databases were searched systematically from inception to February 2026 for studies reporting quality of life outcomes among older adults living with cognitive impairment and hearing and/or vision impairment.  were summarised then categorised by aim. Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria. The limited evidence suggests that (i) individuals living with comorbid vision and cognitive impairments may have substantially worse quality of life than those with either impairment alone, (ii) the effect is similar in size across different quality of life outcomes and (iii) sensory support interventions, involving counselling and assistance with device use, appear to be a more promising method of improving quality of life among this population. Further research is necessary to understand the relationship between hearing and vision impairments and quality of life among people living with cognitive impairment. Recommendations for future research include focusing on dual sensory impairment, utilising mixed  approaches and inclusive selection criteria for people living with dementia. Further development and implementation of sensory support programs, codesigned with individuals with lived experience, is also recommended for improving the quality of life for people living with dementia globally.

records.title: How Filial Piety Shapes Benefit Finding Among Family Caregivers: A Narrative Study Based on Adult Child Caregivers of Older Parents With Dementia
records.abstract: This narrative study explored how Chinese filial piety influences benefit finding among adult child caregivers of parents with dementia in Shanghai. Through in-depth interviews with 15 adult child caregivers of parents predominantly living with moderate dementia, we identified filial piety’s dual role: It strengthened caregivers’ role identity and moral responsibility, inspiring intrinsic motivation that enhanced benefit finding while reshaping intergenerational authority. This transformation guided caregivers to balance familial obligations with personal development in medical, daily care, and institutional care decisions, reinterpreting filial ethics through informed caregiving and emotional connection. By balancing parental well-being, filial responsibility, and caregiver sustainability, participants reconstructed filial piety through meaningful companionship, intergenerational responsibility, and self-care. This reflected an evolution from compliant filial piety to balanced filial piety. These findings highlight how culture shapes benefit finding, with implications for dementia family support that honors ethical traditions while meeting contemporary needs.

records.title: Youthful circulation reshapes age-associated DNA methylation across blood and liver
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Prolonged heterochronic parabiosis (HPB) reduces DNA methylation (DNAm) age in old mice, but how age-opposing methylation changes are organized across tissues and retained after removal of youthful circulation is unclear. We analyzed processed reduced-representation bisulfite sequencing data from 78 blood and liver samples from a published prolonged-HPB experiment. Across 1,008,133 CpGs with at least 10-fold coverage in every sample, we quantified normal-aging and HPB effects, defined directional reversal by effect size, tested exact cross-tissue and post-detachment persistence, and used chromosome-aware null models for overlap and gene-convergence analyses. HPB-associated methylation changes opposed normal aging in blood and liver, including in independent-cohort comparisons that avoided a shared Old-ISO reference. At the primary 10-percentage-point threshold, 22,424 blood and 22,286 liver CpGs were reversed immediately after HPB; 1,792 were shared at identical loci. After two months of recovery, 25,867 blood and 15,437 liver CpGs were reversed, with 1,387 exact shared loci. A 64-CpG cross-tissue core persisted across both time points. Reversed CpGs were depleted from promoters and CpG islands and enriched in gene bodies and open-sea regions. After exact shared CpGs were removed, tissue-specific sites showed a modest excess of nearest-gene convergence (4,716 observed vs 4,215 expected; empirical P≈.001), whereas promoter/gene-body and Gene Ontology convergence were not supported by stricter genomic null models. Youthful circulation produces both conserved and tissue-specific reversal of age-associated methylation. Persistence after detachment and modest cross-tissue genomic-neighborhood convergence suggest that systemic rejuvenation is encoded at multiple levels of epigenomic organization.

records.title: Chronobiology of Aging: Interactions Between Circadian Rhythms, Oxidative Stress, and Inflammation
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Chronodisruption is increasingly recognised as a fundamental driver of biological aging rather than merely a consequence of advancing age. Although substantial evidence links circadian dysfunction with individual age-related diseases, the mechanistic integration of chronodisruption across the hallmarks of aging and its therapeutic implications remains fragmented. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of current evidence describing how age-associated deterioration of the circadian timing system interacts with established hallmarks of aging, including genomic instability, epigenetic alterations, mitochondrial dysfunction, dysregulated nutrient sensing, impaired proteostasis, chronic inflammation, and cellular senescence. This article also incorporates how these interconnected mechanisms contribute to the development and progression of major age-related disorders, including neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic diseases, and cancer, highlighting shared molecular regulators such as BMAL1, CLOCK, PER, CRY, REV-ERBs, SIRT1, AMPK, and mTOR. Although several reviews exist that focus on individual diseases or isolated circadian mechanisms, this review integrates molecular, cellular, and translational evidence into a unified framework linking chronodisruption to systemic aging. This article discusses emerging chronotherapeutic strategies including chrono-phototherapy, chrono-nutrition, chrono-exercise, natural chrono-modulators, chrono-pharmacology, and precision geromedicine that aim to restore circadian homeostasis and improve healthy aging. Collectively, this review identifies circadian rhythm restoration as a promising systems-level therapeutic approach and outlines future directions for integrating chronobiology into precision interventions for age-related diseases.

records.title: Handgrip strength relative to DXA-measured appendicular lean mass and life functioning in older Korean adults: a nationwide cross-sectional study
records.abstract: Muscle strength and muscle quantity may become dissociated with aging, but whether strength relative to directly measured appendicular lean mass is associated with life functioning remains uncertain. We examined whether handgrip strength relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)-measured appendicular lean mass was associated with life functioning in older adults.  This cross-sectional study used nationally representative data from the 2024 Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Participants were 1,133 adults aged 65 years or older with valid DXA-derived appendicular lean mass, maximal handgrip strength, and 10-item Life Functioning Scale (LF-10) data. Within each sex, maximal handgrip strength was regressed on appendicular lean mass using survey weights, and the standardized observed-minus-predicted residual represented relative strength. Survey-weighted regression accounted for sampling weights, strata, and clusters. Secondary, supplementary, and exploratory analyses examined EQ-5D-3L ​utility, phase angle, and falls, respectively.  The fully adjusted analysis included 1,069 participants. Each 1-standard-deviation higher relative strength was associated with a 2.95-point higher LF-10 score (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.08–3.82; P P  In older Korean adults, handgrip strength relative to DXA-measured appendicular lean mass was associated with better life functioning. This population-referenced measure may help characterize functional heterogeneity not apparent from muscle quantity alone but does not establish a diagnostic or clinically actionable index. Prospective and external validation are needed before clinical application.

records.title: Green, Blue, Brown, Gray? The Cognitive Benefits of Natural Environments Among Older Mexican Americans
records.abstract: While studies have linked nature exposure to better cognitive health, little is known about the specific types or amounts needed for health benefits. Many studies regarding the health benefits of nature lack racially and ethnically diverse aging populations and have small sample sizes, limiting their generalizability. This study investigated the relationship between land cover types and cognitive function in older Mexican American adults from Wave 5 (2004–2005) of the Hispanic Established Population for the Epidemiological Study of the Elderly (EPESE) while controlling for individual and area-level covariates.  The analytic sample includes 2,069 participants (>98% of Mexican origin) aged 75 and older residing in 415 census tracts. Latent profile analysis of six land cover classifications at the census tract level identified four types: Dense Developed, Gray mix, Open Space/Agricultural, and Green-mix. Cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Key covariates include individual-level factors (e.g., age, education, and gender) and area-level factors (poverty, unemployment, and home ownership). Linear mixed-effect models adjusted for covariates were used to examine associations between land cover types and cognitive function.  Compared to other land types, individuals in greener mixed areas had better cognitive function, especially among women. Discussion Findings suggest that environments with a mix of natural and built features may enhance cognitive health in older Mexican American women. Future research should explore how specific environmental characteristics contribute to cognitive resilience in this population.

records.title: Using Photovoice With Older Adults in Canada: A Scoping Review of Methodological Applications, Adaptations, and Impacts
records.abstract: Photovoice is increasingly used with older adults to explore lived experience and support change, yet its implementation, adaptation, and pathways to change remain unclear.  To examine photovoice use with older adults in Canada, including , adaptations, participant experiences, knowledge translation activities, and documented change.  Following Joanna Briggs Institute and PRISMA-ScR guidance, five databases were searched through September 2025. Thirty-one publications representing 27 unique studies were included.  Studies addressed diverse age-related topics. Adaptations supported accessibility, technology use, communication, and flexible participation. Participant-level experiences were reported in all 27 studies, interpersonal or group-level processes in 16, and completed dissemination or stakeholder engagement in 11. Two studies reported some organizational or program-level implementation, but neither evaluated its outcomes or sustainability. No study evaluated sustained community-, policy-, or system-level change.  More consistent reporting, participant involvement, and explicit pathways to action are needed to maximize photovoice’s contribution to gerontology.

records.title: From Ageing to Waiting: Cancer as a Second Biographical Rupture in Later Life
records.abstract: Older adults are most affected by cancer, yet their psychosocial experiences remain undertheorized in gerontological oncology. Using Bury’s biographical disruption as a sensitizing concept, this qualitative study develops the notion of “second biographical rupture” to examine how cancer emerges as an additional existential and relational rupture within an already transformative ageing process. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 older adults receiving oncology care in Türkiye. Reflexive thematic analysis showed cancer reshaping identity, autonomy, daily routines, caregiving relationships, and perceptions of dignity, dependency, and social worth. Participants described a transition from “ageing” to “waiting,” marked by suspended futures, heightened mortality awareness, social isolation, and greater reliance on family caregivers, articulating experiences from a later-life position, centred on fear of dependency and a narrowed temporal horizon. Alongside loss and dependency, some reported self-redefinition and renewed self-worth. The findings reveal critical gaps in psychosocial support, care coordination, and age-responsive geriatric oncology services.

records.title: Dementia Care Coordinator Programmes in Primary Care and Community Settings: An International Rapid Review of Reviews
records.abstract: Dementia care coordinator (DCC) programmes are designed to support individuals living with dementia and their unpaid carers to navigate the complex health and social care system, ensuring access to services and information. However, the increasing number of diverse and varied programmes has resulted in a fragmented evidence base, making it challenging for policymakers, commissioners and health services researchers to fully understand and evaluate these initiatives. To address this challenge, this paper presents findings from a rapid review of reviews, designed to explore the current landscape of DCC programmes in primary and community care settings. Using a rapid approach to reviewing literature, this study includes ten evidence syntheses (including systematic, narrative, and scoping reviews) published since 2012. All included evidence syntheses focus on DCC programmes embedded in primary care or a community setting. Critical appraisals were conducted across each of the ten reviews. Findings identified a variety of terms used for DCC programmes, making it difficult to understand whether there is a difference between DCC and case manager roles. Several workforce considerations are highlighted, including the need for appropriate training, knowledge and caseload. There is also evidence to suggest that DCC programmes may improve some clinical outcomes and carer outcomes. Yet this is harder to demonstrate because programmes and their components varied considerably. This review provides decision-makers and stakeholders with a synthesis of an evolving and heterogeneous evidence base, highlighting the characteristics that appear most important for implementation and effectiveness for DCC programmes. However, the review highlights the need for consolidation of terminology, outcome measures and learning from workforce considerations to ensure sustainability of these programmes moving forward.

records.title: Handgrip strength and 4-meter walk performance as practical functional measures of sarcopenia and physiologic reserve in acute hospital care: a prospective cohort study
records.abstract: Functional reserve is difficult to characterize during routine acute hospital care. Sarcopenia is associated with frailty, disability, and mortality, but rapid functional assessment remains underused in hospitalized older adults. We evaluated handgrip strength and 4-meter walk test (4MWT) performance as pragmatic measures of probable sarcopenia and physiologic reserve during acute illness.  We conducted a prospective cohort study of 279 hospitalized adults aged 65–95 years at a tertiary medical center. Handgrip strength was measured using dynamometry; values  Participants with probable sarcopenia were underrepresented in the 4MWT subgroup. In the 169 participants with eligible 4MWT measurements, probable sarcopenia was independently associated with a 1.59-second longer walk time after adjustment for age and sex (95% CI 0.55–2.63; P = 0.003). The IPW estimate was similar (β = 1.62 s, 95% CI 0.49–2.75; P = 0.005). In an exploratory overlapping age-window analysis, concordance was greatest in the 73–84-year interval (AUC = 0.69, bootstrap 95% CI 0.58–0.80).  Handgrip strength is a rapid bedside-feasible measure, whereas the 4MWT is a complementary ward-based assessment for sufficiently mobile and clinically stable hospitalized older adults. These state-dependent measures characterize functional performance and physiologic reserve during acute illness; longitudinal studies are required to determine their relationship to baseline function, recovery, and healthspan outcomes.

records.title: Association between dominant and non-dominant limb concentric quadriceps strength and low skeletal muscle mass index in community-dwelling older adults: a cross-sectional study
records.abstract: Sarcopenia is common in older adults and predicts adverse outcomes. Contemporary consensus definitions use low muscle strength as the entry point for case-finding, but confirmation requires demonstration of low muscle mass, typically quantified by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) or bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), which are not universally accessible. Quadriceps strength is functionally central to lower-limb health and can be objectively measured by concentric dynamometry. However, previous concentric studies in sarcopenia have typically assessed a single, usually dominant, limb, and the relative contribution of the dominant and non-dominant limbs to the association with muscle mass has not been examined. We therefore compared concentric knee muscle performance between the dominant and non-dominant limbs and examined the association of dominant and non-dominant limb quadriceps strength with low skeletal muscle mass index (low SMI) in community-dwelling older adults.  In this cross-sectional study, community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 60 years underwent concentric knee strength testing at an angular velocity of 60°/s. Peak torque, total work, and average power of the quadriceps and hamstrings were measured bilaterally, and the hamstring-to-quadriceps (H: Q) ratio was calculated. Leg dominance was self-reported, and right- and left-side values were reassigned to the dominant and non-dominant limbs. Participants were classified as normal SMI or low SMI using sex-specific Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS) 2019 criteria. Paired t-tests compared dominant and non-dominant limb variables; age- and sex-adjusted binary logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis with DeLong comparison, and a mixed-design (limb SMI group) analysis evaluated the contribution of each limb to low SMI.  A total of 171 participants were included in the analysis (139 normal SMI, 32 low SMI; mean age 69.88 ± 7.97 years). Dominant limb quadriceps peak torque, total work, and average power were significantly greater than the corresponding non-dominant limb values (all p ≤ 0.004), whereas hamstring variables showed no significant between-limb differences. In adjusted models, higher quadriceps peak torque, total work, and average power of the dominant limb were associated with lower odds of low SMI (odds ratios [ORs] 0.968, 0.993, and 0.958; all p ≤ 0.010); in the non-dominant limb, total work and average power were significantly associated (ORs 0.994 and 0.966; p = 0.049 and 0.030), whereas peak torque was not (OR 0.976; p = 0.058). The limb × SMI group interaction was not significant for any quadriceps variable (all p > 0.10). Area-under-the-curve (AUC) values were similar for the dominant (0.63–0.64) and non-dominant limbs (0.60–0.64; all DeLong p ≥ 0.34), and all remained below 0.70.  Lower quadriceps strength in both the dominant and non-dominant limbs was associated with low SMI, and neither limb contributed disproportionately to this association or showed superior discriminative ability. These findings indicate a bilateral reduction in knee-extensor strength that is independent of limb dominance; given the modest discrimination, quadriceps concentric strength should complement, rather than replace, established muscle mass assessment.

records.title: Staff clothing and uniforms in care homes for older people: a scoping review and analysis of online content
records.abstract: Long-term care policy and practice continue to promote institutional living at the expense of support for ageing in place. Improving experiences of care home residents requires recognising care homes as places of everyday living, moving beyond clinical models to support ‘living with care’ rather than ‘existing in care’. Staff uniforms are ubiquitous in care homes yet remain relatively unexamined. Unlike hospitals, care homes are places where older people live, and uniforms may contribute to the medicalisation of ageing. Non-uniform approaches could support home-like environments and resident wellbeing. An emerging trend of non-uniform dress codes in UK care homes warrants evidence synthesis.  We conducted a scoping review in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines, searching six bibliographic databases to April 2026. Supplementary searches of care sector websites, charity platforms, and public discussion forums captured perspectives beyond academic literature. Included sources spanned empirical studies and non-academic public content addressing staff clothing in care homes for older adults.  Fifty-eight records were included, describing 13 empirical studies and 36 public discourse cases; only a minority of research records (8; 35%) were peer-reviewed. Seven themes were identified: health and hygiene; identification, care home atmosphere; changing behaviours; perspectives and preferences; perceptions and connotations; and decision making. Despite a limited evidence base, available research suggests non-uniform policies do not compromise hygiene or resident health, and may reduce anxiety, support independence and foster relational, homelike environments. Public discourse presented a more contested picture, with both approaches carrying perceived advantages and tensions.  Staff clothing is a socially embedded aspect of care practice. Research evidence suggests non-uniform policies do not compromise safety and may actively support resident wellbeing and relational engagement. However, public discourse reflects genuine concerns around professionalism, identification and individuality that empirical research has not fully addressed. Context-sensitive, resident-centred decision making and research prioritising direct engagement with residents are needed.

records.title: Health technology innovation in long-term care of older people: Advancing a policy-relevant research agenda
records.abstract: As the mean age of the world’s population rises, there is increasing demand for long-term post-acute care (LTPAC), where health information technology (HIT) has potential to improve care quality, access, and equity. However, evidence guiding effective HIT implementation in LTPAC remains limited. Authors of this paper report on proceedings from the International Summit on Innovation and Technology in Care of Older People (IS-ITCOP) and present a consensus-driven policy-relevant research agenda to advance HIT use in LTPAC. A two-day international summit convened 47 experts in research, policy, clinical care, and technology. Plenary sessions with keynotes and facilitated discussion groups addressed four domains: emerging care models and technology, workforce of the future, transparency and accountability, and safety and privacy. Data from recordings, structured notes, and word cloud visualization were synthesized to identify consensus-based research priorities. Key priorities include developing equitable and interoperable technology-enabled care models; strengthening workforce readiness through digital competencies, informatics leadership, and training; redesigning accountability systems to reduce reporting burden and improve data validity; and addressing ethical, privacy, cybersecurity, and consent concerns. Cross-cutting themes highlighted infrastructure limitations, policy misalignment, workforce shortages, and disparities in technology access across settings. Advancing HIT in LTPAC requires coordinated policy, infrastructure, workforce, and governance strategies. Findings support the need for investment in interoperability, workforce development, equitable technology design, and person-centered implementation approaches to improve quality, safety, and outcomes for older adults receiving long-term care.

records.title: Ageist attitudes as a moderator of objective and subjective vision: A longitudinal study
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This longitudinal study examined the relationship between  visual acuity and subjective vision over a six-month period. Specifically, it investigated the moderating role of internalized ageist attitudes in shaping how  vision relates to perceived sensory vision difficulties over time.  A sample of 139 community-dwelling participants (M=70.25, SD=5.57) underwent  vision assessments (distance and near visual acuity, and contrast sensitivity) and completed the Fraboni Scale of Ageism at baseline (T1). Subjective vision assessments were conducted at T1 and six months later (T2). Hierarchical regression analyses were used to predict T2 subjective vision, controlling for baseline subjective vision, age, sex, relationship status, and self-rated health.  No direct main effect of T1  vision on T2 subjective vision was found. However, higher baseline ageist attitudes significantly predicted poorer subjective vision at T2 (β=.14, p=.041). Crucially, a significant interaction emerged (β=.16, p=.018);  vision at T1 predicted poorer subjective vision at T2 only among individuals with high levels of ageist attitudes. For those with low ageist attitudes, this association was non-significant. Discussion These findings support Stereotype Embodiment Theory, suggesting that internalized ageist stereotypes asct as a cognitive lens through which individuals interpret biological sensory cues. The  indicate that subjective vision is not merely a reflection of physical decline but is significantly shaped by psychological frameworks. Clinical interventions aimed at reducing internalized ageist attitudes may mitigate the negative subjective experience of vision loss, potentially reducing functional vulnerabilities and enhancing overall well-being.

records.title: Factors Influencing Financial Exploitation Vulnerability Among Older Adults
records.abstract: Financial exploitation of older adults such as elder theft and scams is a growing public health and social concern, yet factors contributing to exploitation vulnerability remain insufficiently understood.  This study examined associations among various factors including sociodemographic characteristics, financial literacy, financial skills, depression, social networks, technology anxiety, and financial exploitation vulnerability in older adults.  A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 109 community-dwelling older adults. Hierarchical regression analyses examined predictors of financial exploitation vulnerability after controlling for sociodemographic characteristics.  Lower household income, weaker financial skills, higher depression levels, and non-Caucasian race were significantly associated with greater financial exploitation vulnerability. Financial skills emerged as the strongest modifiable predictor. These findings support multidimensional prevention strategies that strengthen financial competencies while addressing mental health. The findings also inform future research on technology-assisted approaches to identifying and preventing financial exploitation among older adults.

records.title: Fear of Falling and Indicators of Psychological and Physical Vulnerability in Socially Engaged Middle-Aged and Older Adults
records.abstract: Fear of falling (FoF) is common among older adults, but its relevance in socially engaged populations remains unclear.  To compare cognitive, psychological, and physical function outcomes between participants with high and low FoF and examine associations between FoF and vulnerability indicators.  This cross-sectional study included 120 adults aged ≥50 years enrolled in a community-based active aging program. FoF was assessed using the Falls Efficacy Scale-International. Cognitive function, depressive symptoms, and physical function were evaluated using validated questionnaires and performance-based tests.  Participants with high FoF showed lower cognitive performance (adjusted mean difference = −1.41; p = 0.031), greater depressive symptoms (1.33; p = 0.006), and reduced handgrip strength (−3.43 kg; p = 0.020). No significant differences were observed in physical activity levels or most functional outcomes, suggesting that FoF may reveal relevant vulnerability even when conventional activity and functional measures appear preserved.

records.title: Cognitive Decline and Consumption Changes Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults
records.abstract: Cognitive impairment is associated with financial burdens on individuals and their families, yet less is known about how families change consumption patterns around the onset of cognitive decline beyond out-of-pocket medical expenditures. Using data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and the Consumption and Activities Mail Survey (CAMS) from 2002 to 2018, we examined changes in spending during the six years before and after the first onset of cognitive impairment no dementia (CIND) and dementia among community-dwelling older adults. We found that older adults with cognitive decline reduced total spending, as well as spending on food at home and away from home and on non-durables, before and after onset. Out-of-pocket medical expenses, transportation, and housing spending remained unchanged, but there is suggestive evidence of declines in leisure spending, gift-giving, and utility costs. Future research should explore the potential for material deprivation related to these consumption changes.

records.title: Understanding and Prioritizing Needs of People With Young-Onset Dementia and Family Carers Across the Disease Trajectory: A Qualitative Study and Conceptual Framework
records.abstract: People with young-onset dementia and their family carers have unique needs, as a dementia diagnosis at a younger age profoundly impacts work, family life, and social roles. Understanding these needs is essential to develop tailored psychosocial support. This study aimed at creating a conceptual framework of needs related to young-onset dementia by exploring and prioritizing needs across different phases: before diagnosis, shortly after diagnosis, and long term. Focus groups were conducted with persons living with young-onset dementia and their family carers. Inductive qualitative analysis informed a conceptual framework, while descriptive, aggregated scores of ‘prioritization cards’ identified the urgency of needs. Before diagnosis, the most urgent need for the persons themselves and family carers was clarity, particularly regarding the diagnostic process and access to a clear care pathway. Shortly after diagnosis, key needs included coping with the diagnosis, navigating post-diagnostic support, and planning for the future, with family carers prioritizing a timely and tailored point of contact and persons living with young-onset dementia seeking clarity about disease progression. In the long term, needs focused on balancing care and autonomy within the dyad, sustaining life at home, managing transitions to residential care, and finding a meaningful way to spend the day. Family carers emphasized administrative support and persons themselves mostly valued positivity. The needs and priorities of persons living with young-onset dementia and their family carers evolve across the disease trajectory, with shifting and interdependent needs. Differences in perspectives highlight the necessity of dyadic and family-centered approaches. These insights can guide the development of tailored psychosocial interventions that address timely, phase-specific needs and support both the person living with young-onset dementia and their family.

records.title: Implementing community-based heat-health interventions for older adults: a comparative case study of two NGO delivery models in Hong Kong
records.abstract: Extreme heat is an increasing threat to the health and wellbeing of older adults, particularly those living in densely populated urban environments with poor housing conditions and limited access to cooling resources. Community-based heat-health interventions have been proposed as an important climate adaptation strategy to reduce heat-related vulnerability among older adults, yet little is known about how such interventions are implemented in real-world settings.  This qualitative case study examined how two nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) implemented a community-based heat-health intervention for vulnerable older adults in Hong Kong. Data were drawn from observations of 51 home visits and 7 community activities, case conference notes, and four semi-structured focus groups with frontline and management staff ( n = 18). Inductive thematic analysis was used to explore how organizational approaches, local contexts, and service-delivery models shaped implementation.  Although both NGOs implemented the same core intervention components, they adopted different service-delivery models. NGO 1 employed a relationship-centered approach emphasizing continuity of care, individualized assessment, and trust-building. This approach facilitated rapport-building, individualized support, and identification of misconceptions and environmental risks, but required substantial staff time and resources to maintain continuity of care and individualized engagement. NGO 2 adopted a standardized, outreach-oriented model designed to maximize community outreach, visibility, and awareness. This approach increased visibility and facilitated broad distribution of cooling resources but was sometimes constrained by the diverse housing conditions and complex needs of older adults. Housing characteristics, social isolation, and environmental constraints influenced how both approaches were implemented in practice. Collaboration with an academic team supported ongoing adaptation and capacity building throughout implementation.  Community-based heat-health interventions can play an important role in protecting older adults from heat-related health risks and supporting climate adaptation in ageing populations, but different delivery models involve distinct implementation strengths and challenges. Relationship-centered approaches may be particularly valuable when ongoing assessment, trust-building, and individualized support are required, whereas outreach-oriented approaches may promote awareness of heat-health risks and community engagement. The findings highlight the importance of aligning intervention strategies with the needs and living environments of older adults and suggest that community-based adaptation efforts should be accompanied by broader policies addressing housing-related heat vulnerability. Clinical trial number not applicable.

records.title: Household fuel type, kitchen ventilation, and frailty trajectory membership among older adults: a community-based longitudinal study in Nanjing, China
records.abstract: Longitudinal evidence jointly considering household fuel type and kitchen ventilation in relation to frailty trajectory membership among older adults remains limited. This study aimed to identify frailty index (FI) trajectories among community-dwelling older adults and examine their associations with household fuel type and kitchen ventilation.  We analysed annual health examination data from 2020 to 2023 for 47,947 community-dwelling adults aged 65 years or older in Nanjing, China, with at least three valid FI assessments. Frailty was measured using a 34-item FI. Latent class mixed models identified FI trajectories. Multivariable multinomial logistic regression examined the associations of baseline household fuel type and kitchen ventilation with trajectory membership.  Three trajectories were identified: low-level progressive (26.47%), moderate-level gradual-increase (51.33%) and high-level persistent-burden (22.20%). They differed mainly in sustained FI levels, with modest increases over follow-up. With the low FI trajectory as the reference, solid fuel use versus clean fuel use among participants with ventilation was associated with membership in the moderate and high FI trajectories, with adjusted relative risk ratios (RRRs) of 1.496 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.400–1.598) and 2.230 (95% CI 2.061–2.414), respectively. Among clean fuel users, the corresponding RRRs for absence versus presence of ventilation were 1.252 (95% CI 1.165–1.346) and 1.614 (95% CI 1.479–1.761). Analyses of follow-up FI adjusted for baseline FI supported these associations.  Solid fuel use among participants with kitchen ventilation and absence of ventilation among clean fuel users were associated with membership in higher-FI trajectories. These findings support considering both fuel type and ventilation when assessing household environments in older populations. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

records.title: Aging Service Organizational Capacity to Deliver Evidence-Based Depression Programs: A National Survey
records.abstract: Integration of mental health programs within community-based, social or aging service organizations has been recommended to serve more older adults with depression.  The purpose of this study was to obtain input from aging service organizations across the United States regarding their consideration and resource needs for implementing a lay-led program for depression ( “Do More, Feel Better,” DMFB).  An online survey distributed via email inquired about perceived need and consideration regarding DMFB, existing resources, and resource needs.  Among 242 respondents across 42 states, perceived need for community-based depression services was high (8.7/10), and almost all reported they would consider implementing DMFB (94%). Most had some resources in place to support DMFB (e.g., technology, staff, experience with other evidence-based programs), but most indicated need for key program-specific resources, with the most critical resource needs being funding, dedicated personnel, and training (e.g., depression identification, DMFB delivery, and emergency management).

records.title: Barriers and Facilitators to Technology Use Among Caregivers of Homebound Older Adults: Descriptive Qualitative Study
records.abstract: Homebound older adults (≥60 y) and their informal family caregivers face multiple challenges in meeting their instrumental, emotional, and informational needs, which result in lower functional status, multiple comorbidities, and poorer mental health. Caregivers are tasked with providing uncompensated care for medically complex older adults, often without formal health care training. This circumstance may translate to high levels of burden and greater vulnerability to social isolation and loneliness, which may precipitate chronic stress and compromise caregiver health. In recent years, numerous health-focused technologies assisting with health-promoting behaviors such as physical activity, stress management, and nutritional tracking have emerged. However, little is known about how these tools are adopted by family caregivers of homebound older adults.  This descriptive qualitative study aimed to explore how caregivers of homebound older adults perceive technology in the context of supporting caregiving and aging in place through focus groups and one-on-one interviews.  We conducted a descriptive qualitative study using in-person and online video conference focus group methodology with 40 individuals (32 caregivers, 6 clinicians, and 2 additional key informants) to explore perspectives on caregivers’ use of technology to support their caregiving activities. Participants completed a brief sociodemographic questionnaire prior to all interviews. Procedures for thematic analysis were used to analyze the data and identify emerging themes.  Three main themes (and related subthemes) emerged from the data: (1) these technologies are not designed for people like us, (2) balancing the scales, and (3) preserving a sense of self. Caregivers’ experiences with technology are marked by a paradox: the same technologies that can ease caregiving activities may also impose new burdens through additional costs, uncertainty, learning demands, and emotional strain.  Caregivers should not navigate these technological tensions alone. Realizing the promise of technology requires more than innovative tools—it demands caregiver-centered design, accessible and equitable implementation strategies, and sustained clinical and health system support to ensure that technology alleviates, rather than amplifies, caregiver burden.

records.title: Marital Status, Living Arrangement, and Aging Well in China
records.abstract: This study explores the relationship between marital status, living arrangements, and aging well among Chinese adults aged 50 and older.  Using data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), we developed a multidimensional measure of aging well (physiological, functional, cognitive, psychological, and subjective). Analysis was based on a five-category typology of marital and living arrangements.  A clear hierarchy emerged in the findings: married individuals co-residing with spouses experienced the most favorable outcomes, while unmarried individuals living alone faced the greatest challenges. Non-traditional arrangements (e.g., married living apart) also showed significant difficulties, particularly in subjective well-being. These associations were moderated by socio-demographic factors, with disparities being less pronounced among respondents aged 75+, retirees, urban residents, and those with healthier lifestyles. Discussion The findings underscore the enduring importance of co-resident marital relationships while highlighting the evolving influence of diverse family arrangements on the well-being of older adults in China.

records.title: Social Return on Investment (SROI) of the BrainTrack App for Monitoring Brain Health Among Older Australians
records.abstract: Timely diagnosis of dementia is critical, as early identification enables interventions that can meaningfully improve quality of life and support long-term planning for individuals and their families. Despite this, many Australians continue to receive a diagnosis at a late stage due to a range of personal, social, and structural barriers. BrainTrack, a freely available and evidence-based mobile application, was developed to help address this gap by supporting users to monitor their cognitive health and encouraging earlier engagement with healthcare professionals when concerns arise. This study sought to assess the broader social and economic value generated by BrainTrack. A Social Return on Investment (SROI) framework was employed to quantify the social outcomes associated with the app. Survey data collected 12 months after initial use captured five key outcomes: increased dementia literacy, enhanced dementia knowledge, reduced stigma, greater motivation to adopt cognitive health-promoting behaviours, and increased help-seeking intentions. Monetary values were assigned to each outcome to estimate the value created. Inputs included the resources invested in BrainTrack, such as initial development costs and ongoing maintenance. To determine the net impact, adjustments were made for deadweight, displacement, attribution, and drop-off prior to calculating the SROI ratio. Survey responses from 2,339 BrainTrack users informed the analysis. With an investment of AU$1.9 million over five years, the SROI analysis estimated a social return of approximately $5 for every $1 invested in BrainTrack. Sensitivity analyses showed ratios ranging from AU$0.86:1 to AU$24:1. The largest proportion of estimated social value was associated with increased motivation to change, whereas reduced stigma and increased help-seeking were associated with comparatively smaller estimated social value. Overall, BrainTrack was associated with social and economic value through cognitive self-monitoring, increased dementia awareness, and greater engagement with health services.

records.title: Immediate task-specific and delayed generalized adaptations to variable dual-task training in community-dwelling older adults: a randomized waitlist-controlled trial
records.abstract: Aging is accompanied by progressive declines in cognitive and physical function. Dual-task training, which combines cognitive and motor demands, is a promising nonpharmacological approach, yet evidence that its benefits generalize beyond trained tasks and persist over time remains limited. This study examined the immediate and longer-term effects of a variable dual-task intervention on motor and cognitive function in community-dwelling older adults.  Fifty adults aged ≥ 65 years, including participants meeting criteria for mild cognitive impairment, were randomly allocated to an intervention group (IG; n = 30) or waitlist control (WLC; n = 20). The IG completed a 12-week, twice-weekly program (24 sessions × 60 min) designed to be highly variable across cognitive and motor demands to minimize task-specific learning. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and three-month follow-up, including the Timed Up and Go Test, Five Times Sit-to-Stand Test (5xSTS), Eriksen Flanker Test, Trail Making Test, and Digit Span Test. Between-group effects and long-term trajectories within the IG were analyzed using linear and generalized linear mixed models under an intention-to-treat approach.  The intervention produced a significant improvement in functional lower-limb strength relative to the WLC at post-intervention (5xSTS: Group × Time interaction p = 0.005, standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.54), maintained within the IG at three-month follow-up. No significant between-group effects were observed for the remaining motor or cognitive outcomes at post-intervention. Within the IG, improvements in functional mobility (Timed Up and Go, SMD = 0.28), inhibitory control (Flanker reaction time, SMD = 0.40–0.42), and short-term memory (forward Digit Span, SMD = 0.62) were absent immediately post-intervention and emerged only at follow-up.  Variable dual-task training produced immediate gains in functional lower-limb strength that persisted at follow-up, alongside delayed improvements in functional mobility, inhibitory control, and short-term memory consistent with a post-training consolidation process. These findings suggest two complementary pathways: task-specific overlap between training and assessment may explain the immediate motor gains, whereas variable practice may foster broader cognitive and mobility benefits that emerge over time. Trial registration German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00038787 ( https://www.drks.de/DRKS00038787 ), retrospectively registered on 19/12/2025.

records.title: Heat-related symptom worsening, cooling constraints, and care disruption among older cardiology outpatients: a convergent mixed-methods study
records.abstract: Hot weather is an established cardiovascular hazard, but patient-level evidence on how clinical vulnerability, cooling constraints and barriers to care interact in older cardiology outpatients remains limited.  We conducted a convergent mixed- study in the cardiology outpatient clinic of a tertiary university hospital in Zonguldak, Türkiye, from June to August 2026. A total of 680 consecutively recruited patients aged ≥ 65 years completed a structured interviewer-administered survey covering heat-related symptoms, housing and cooling capacity, health-care access and frailty assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS). The primary outcome was self-reported heat-related worsening of cardiovascular symptoms; secondary outcomes included care delay and marked impact on daily life. Multivariable logistic regression was used, and a pragmatic seven-domain heat-vulnerability index was explored. Twenty purposively sampled participants underwent semi-structured interviews, analysed thematically and integrated with the quantitative findings.  Mean age was 71.3 ± 5.3 years and 48.1% were women. Inadequate effective cooling was reported by 82.4%, at least two heat-related symptoms by 75.9%, and heat-related care delay by 30.9%. Among participants giving a definite response, 52.1% reported symptom worsening, independently associated with heart failure (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.86, 95% CI 1.18–2.95), prolonged hot indoor exposure (aOR 1.82, 1.19–2.81), summer transport difficulty (aOR 1.65, 1.08–2.53) and greater frailty (aOR per CFS point 1.30, 1.09–1.55). Care delay was associated with limited or absent daytime support (aOR 2.99, 2.05–4.35), transport difficulty (aOR 2.59, 1.67–4.00), living alone (aOR 2.45, 1.62–3.70) and insufficient income (aOR 2.02, 1.34–3.03). Symptom worsening, care delay and daily-life impact increased across vulnerability categories. Interviews showed that effective cooling, access to care and social support depended on their practical usability rather than nominal availability.  Heat-related burden in older cardiology outpatients extends beyond acute events to symptoms, daily functioning and continuity of care, consistent with a multidimensional pattern of clinical, environmental and social vulnerability. Frailty, effective cooling, transport and reliable support may be relevant domains for brief heat-health discussions in outpatient cardiovascular care. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

records.title: Changes in Patterns of Health Care Use Among Older Adults in Singapore Across a Decade: Repeated Nationwide Cross-Sectional Survey
records.abstract: There is limited evidence on the patterns of health care use among older adults in Singapore over the past decade.  This study examines whether the proportion of specific services used within sociodemographic subgroups, the factors associated with health care use, and the network structure of health care use have changed over a decade.  We used data from 2 repeated nationwide cross-sectional surveys of Singapore residents aged 60 years and older, conducted in 2013 (n=2565) and 2023 (n=2010). Health care service use was obtained from an adapted version of the Client Service Receipt Inventory and analyzed using multivariable logistic regression and network analysis.  The most significant changes between 2013 and 2023 were in the proportions of older adults who had consulted private hospital/clinic doctors (decreased by 4.6 percentage points; n=655, 26.5% vs n=425, 21.9%; P =.02), consulted public and private dentists (increased by 6.4 percentage points; n=215, 11.6% vs n=269, 18%; P P  This study provides important data on population-level changes in health care usage among older adults across the decade from 2013 to 2023, which will help policymakers ensure better health care delivery for older adults.

records.title: Operationalizing Cognitive Frailty: A Systematic Review of Definitions, Tools, and Measurement Inconsistencies
records.abstract: and  Cognitive frailty (CF), the co-occurrence of physical frailty and cognitive impairment without dementia, is a potentially reversible condition associated with adverse outcomes in older adults. However, heterogeneity in operational definitions and measurement approaches limits comparability and clinical translation. This review examined how CF has been defined and operationalized, including adaptations to established criteria. Research Design and  PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycINFO were searched for English-language studies published from 2013 through 2025. Eligible studies explicitly referred to CF in adults aged 50 years or older. Risk of bias was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Definitions, assessment tools, thresholds, and operational criteria were synthesized descriptively. Fried Phenotype (FP) implementation was examined using an adaptation-equivalence typology classifying domain-level measurement and threshold deviations.  Among 257 studies, 13 frailty and 26 cognitive assessment tools were identified. The FP was predominantly utilized (n = 164/257; 64%), although 68% (n = 112/164) modified the measurement method, threshold, or both in at least one domain. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) thresholds used to define cognitive impairment varied substantially, whereas all studies using the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) used a threshold of 0.5. Dementia was not explicitly excluded in 50 studies, despite its exclusion being a defining criterion of CF.  CF remains operationally heterogeneous. Updated international consensus and minimum reporting standards are needed to clarify core criteria and acceptable adaptations. FP-based studies should explicitly report domain-level modifications to improve comparability, reproducibility, and evidence synthesis.

records.title: Disruptions in Support Networks of People Living With Dementia: Evidence From a National Study of Caregiver Networks
records.abstract: People living with dementia rely on informal support that may be especially vulnerable to social restrictions such as those imposed during the COVID-19 pandemic.  To assess whether family and friends supporting adults with dementia were more likely to discontinue assistance during the pandemic than those supporting adults with other chronic conditions.  Using nationally representative data from 2,037 U.S. current caregivers reporting on 7,742 supporters within their care networks, multilevel logistic regression identified factors associated with discontinued support.  Ten percent of supporters withdrew help. Those assisting care recipients with dementia had higher odds of withdrawal (OR = 1.40, 95% CI 1.02–1.92). Supporters who were friends or distant relatives of the caregiver were more likely to withdraw than those who were close family, while strongly connected or dual-role supporters were less likely to withdraw (OR = 0.07, 95% CI 0.05–0.10). Higher caregiver income buffered against loss.

records.title: Parental Longevity and Cognitive Ability in Older Mexican Adults
records.abstract: Parental longevity is linked to better offspring cognition, with limited evidence from middle-income countries. We examined associations between parental longevity and cognition in Mexico while controlling for health, socioeconomic status (SES), and genetic factors.  We used the 2018 wave of the Mexican Health and Aging Study ( n = 5,049; age 65+). Maternal/paternal longevity was based on survival to age 85 or older. We used latent variable regressions to estimate associations with offspring cognition, adjusting for demographics, parental characteristics, health, health behaviors, SES, and APOE-ε4 carrier status.  About 31% of respondents had a mother and 31% had a father who survived to age 85 or older. Maternal, but not paternal, longevity was independently associated with better offspring cognition. The maternal association persisted after full adjustment.  Maternal longevity was positively linked to offspring cognition independent of health, health behaviors, SES, and APOE-ε4. Intergenerational support and broader genetic factors may contribute to this association.

records.title: Effects of professional trainer-led and trained volunteer-led bodyweight training programs on physical fitness and body composition of rural community-dwelling older adults
records.abstract: and  Physical inactivity accelerates functional decline in rural older adults with limited exercise resources. Although bodyweight training is scalable, whether benefits depend on professional supervision remains unclear. We compared professional- and trained volunteer-led bodyweight training programs (BWTP) on functional fitness and body composition in rural community-dwelling older adults. Research Design and  In this quasi-experimental, community-based, three-group pretest-posttest study with community-level allocation (April 2021-January 2022), adults aged ≥65 years who were independent in activities of daily living and not engaged in other regular exercise programs were assigned to a professional trainer, trained volunteer, or comparison group. The intervention groups received a 12-week BWTP. Functional fitness and body composition were assessed pre- and postintervention, and Group × Time effects were examined using two-way mixed ANOVA.  Among 72 participants (Professional Trainer Group, PTG, n = 25; Volunteer Trainer Group, VTG, n = 22; Comparison Group, CG, n = 25), several functional fitness outcomes showed significant Group × Time interactions (p ≤ .003; partial η² = .155-.248). Both intervention groups improved mobility and postural stability more than the CG. PTG improved handgrip strength versus CG (Hedges’ g = 0.85), whereas VTG showed the largest lower-limb muscular endurance gain (g = 1.26). CG declined in several functional measures. No body-composition outcome remained significant after adjustment.  Trained volunteer-led BWTP may extend exercise delivery and support functional fitness in resource-limited rural communities. Hybrid models with professional oversight warrant evaluation because body-composition effects did not persist after multiplicity adjustment.

records.title: Finding the upsides to living alone: Adaptation and inequality among older U.S. adults?
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This study investigates how the growing population of older Americans living alone adapts to daily life, testing three sociological hypotheses regarding “upsides” to solo living: spending more time outside, spending more time with non-residential ties, and spending more time in organized activities. We also consider whether such adaptations are unequal, investigating potential fault lines across key social categories including race/ethnicity, education, gender, and disability.  Using 2003–2019 American Time Use Survey data (N = 83,997), we employed multiple regression analysis to estimate both the likelihood of participation and the duration of time spent in each of these ways.   support the notion of locational and social adaptation: older adults living alone spend significantly more time outside the home and more time with friends and non-residential family than their co-resident peers. However, we found that solo dwellers spend less time in organized activities. Consistent with one dimension of the unequal adaptation hypothesis, several behavioral patterns were stratified by race/ethnicity, with Black older adults standing out from each of the other groups. Discussion Findings point to living alone as a distinct social ecology rather than a simple marker of deficit, with older adults adapting through the reorganization of daily exposure to people and places. This adaptation does not appear strongly structured by most social categories, though strong racialized differences suggest that future research should continue to assess the way diverse older Americans live together and with others.

records.title: Unraveling the Early-Life Influences on Healthy Aging: Insights From the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS)
records.abstract: To examine the association between early-life circumstances and healthy aging among community-dwelling older Chinese adults.  Data were from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. We used regression  to identify independent and joint associations of six early-life factors with healthy aging as assessed by the Chinese Healthy Aging Index (CHAI; 0–12), a composite score evaluating six physiological systems.  Of 3,069 participants, 4.82% had the healthiest CHAI score (0–2). After multivariable adjustment, personal education and family economic status were associated with healthier CHAI individually; the cumulative early-life score was associated with the CHAI, both dichotomously and continuously. Each additional score was associated with 37% (95% CI: 23%, 53%) higher odds of being in the healthiest CHAI category. Discussion Favorable early-life socioeconomic conditions support healthier aging among Chinese older adults, highlighting the need to address early-life inequalities to promote healthy aging.

records.title: What Determines the Preference to Coreside? Applying the Andersen-Newman Framework to a Lagged Longitudinal Analysis Among Older Adults in China
records.abstract: Using longitudinal data, we investigate changes in coresidence preference of Chinese older adults and, with application of the Andersen-Newman framework, examine factors contributing to coresidence preference.  Data come from five waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey collected between 2005 and 2018. A random-effect model uses baseline covariates to predict coresidence preference at follow-up between two adjacent waves, controlling for baseline preference and changes in actual living arrangement between baseline and follow-up.  Regressions showed enabling factors played a more robust role in shaping coresidence preference than time-invariant personal characteristics. Interactions found that some personal characteristics reinforced the effect of enabling factors. Discussion Coresidence is not necessarily the most sought-after living arrangement among older Chinese. What is regarded as “traditional” may instead reflect circumstantial factors, such that a coresidential living arrangement is best suited to an older person’s particular situation.
