records.title: Fertility and Later-Life Mental Health: Evidence on Transfers and Instrumental Assistance From Adult Children in Indonesia
records.abstract: This study examined whether completed fertility shapes later-life mental health in Indonesia and whether adult children’s support explains this relationship.  Using the 2007 and 2014 Indonesian Family Life Survey, we instrumented fertility with differential exposure to Village Contraceptive Distribution Centers and estimated 2SLS and instrumental-variables mediation models.  An additional child reduced CES-D score and probability of elevated depressive symptoms. Financial and material transfers formed a protective pathway, while the remaining component outside measured transfers offset part of this effect. Higher fertility also increased instrumental assistance, although its mediating contribution was imprecisely estimated. Protective effects were more apparent among respondents with less than primary education, alongside adverse physical and nutritional outcomes. Discussion Completed fertility may improve later-life mental health partly through transfers from adult children, while supportive and burdensome consequences coexist, especially among socioeconomically constrained older adults. Estimates apply to the fertility-responsive population identified by the IV design.

records.title: Identification of Novel Protein Biomarkers and Lifestyle-Modifiable Targets for Osteoporosis: Evidence from Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization Analyses
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Osteoporosis (OP), a degenerative bone disease prevalent in aging populations, can lead to various complications and significantly impair the quality of life of elderly patients. We aimed to identify OP-related protein biomarkers and modifiable lifestyle factors for OP prevention in older adults.  Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) and colocalization analyses were conducted to assess the possible causal effects of plasma protein on OP. Genetic data for plasma proteins were derived from the deCODE (4907 proteins) and UK Biobank-PPP (2923 proteins) datasets. OP summary statistics were obtained from the FinnGen study (10,461 cases). Two-sample Mendelian randomization (TSMR) analyses were subsequently performed to evaluate the effects of lifestyle factors on OP-related proteins.  Primary SMR analysis identified 31 and 24 OP-related proteins in the deCODE and UKB-PPP cohorts, respectively. Cross-analysis of both datasets identified nine OP-related plasma protein targets. Among them, RSPO3 showed moderate evidence of colocalization with OP (PP.H4 = 0.643). TSMR analysis suggested that genetically predicted higher body mass index (BMI) was associated with increased RSPO3 levels (β = 0.08, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.14, p = 0.001), whereas type 2 diabetes (T2DM) was associated with lower RSPO3 levels (β = -5.71, 95% CI -11.16 to -0.26, p = 0.045).  This study identified nine plasma protein biomarkers with genetic evidence supporting their association with OP risk, with RSPO3 showing the strongest supportive evidence among the prioritized targets. These findings offer new insights into OP etiology and highlight how metabolic traits may influence bone health via specific protein mediators.

records.title: Economic evaluation of the annual and daily costs of the adult foster care model for older dependent adults: Insights from the Karukera Study of Aging in Foster Families
records.abstract: and  Adult foster care may represent a viable alternative to nursing homes for dependent older adults. This study aimed to estimate the annual and daily cost of adult foster care for older adults. Research Design and  The Karukera Study of Aging in Foster Families is a prospective, one-year observational study including adults aged 60+ living in adult foster care in the French Caribbean Islands. We measured healthcare resource utilization using the RUD (Resource Utilization in Dementia)-Lite instrument. Costs related to healthcare consumption, foster caregiver remuneration, and training were estimated and expressed per patient-year.  A total of 106 older adults (mean age: 82.2±11.2 years; 61.3% women) were followed for one year (mean follow-up duration: 306.1±90.8 days). The daily cost of outpatient care was estimated at €33.3, of which €29.9 corresponded to community nursing visits. Caregiver remuneration and training represented a daily expenditure of €62.8 per older adult. The total annual cost of adult foster care was estimated at €35,076, or €96.1 per resident per day. Hospitalization costs were estimated at €224.0 per patient-year, while emergency department visits accounted for €42.0 per patient-year.  Compared with a daily cost of €121 per resident in metropolitan nursing homes and €150 per resident in nursing homes in the French Caribbean Islands, adult foster care reduced costs by 20.6% and 35.9%, respectively. In the context of constrained healthcare budgets and increasing demand for long-term care related to dependency, adult foster care may represent a scalable and economically sustainable alternative. Clinical Trial Registration NCT04545775

records.title: Development and Evaluation of WELSH: An Institution-Linked Mobile Application for Older Adults in Senior Welfare Centers During COVID-19
records.abstract: COVID-19 closures of South Korean senior welfare centers isolated older adults. We developed and evaluated “WELSH,” an age-friendly, institution-linked mobile app, using the ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) framework.  Following needs assessments, WELSH was implemented across five Seoul centers. During a 2-week pilot, 376 older adults completed pre- and post-intervention questionnaires evaluating usability, digital literacy, and psychosocial indicators (social support, loneliness, depression).  Participants positively rated WELSH’s usability (M = 2.95/4), particularly for accessing center-linked information. Digital literacy scores significantly increased ( p  WELSH successfully maintained institutional connectivity and enhanced short-term digital competence. Practical Implications: This ADDIE-guided process provides a replicable framework for community centers to design age-friendly digital services, ensuring care continuity during crises.

records.title: The Experiences of Psychotherapy for People With Dementia: A Qualitative Interview Study With Family Members
records.abstract: Psychotherapeutic interventions can support people with dementia. Family members often play a pivotal role in the therapeutic process but little is known about their experiences of therapy, how they perceive the impact on their relative, and how the experience affects them directly. This study aimed to explore the experiences of family members who engage in therapy, or support someone living with dementia to attend therapy. Individuals with dementia and their family members were recruited as participants through NHS Trusts, professional networks, social media and community and support groups based in England and Wales. Semi-structured qualitative individual or dyadic interviews were conducted with 17 participants, eight of whom were living with dementia and nine were family members. Framework analysis was used. Family members highlighted “the importance of feeling seen” as distinct individuals by clinicians when engaging with psychotherapy, and not just the carer of their partner. When working with “dementia as dynamic phenomenon”, therapeutic approaches needed to balance being sufficiently structured and containing whilst allowing for adaptions to each individual changeable presentation. Participants highlighted how psychotherapy presented “expected and unexpected outcomes”, challenges that arose when outcomes were not agreed upon, and how therapy functioned as a support structure in ways the participants did not foresee. Psychotherapeutic intervention provides meaningful support to the family members of individuals with dementia. Understanding the needs of family members, alongside the needs of the individual with dementia, and taking a systemic approach is conducive to better therapeutic outcomes. The changeable nature of dementia presentation means that a therapeutic approach should be flexible based on the needs of the family. Psychotherapeutic intervention with individuals with dementia can have a range of benefits for the individual and the wider family, when sufficient considerations are made to understand each person’s needs.

records.title: Joint associations of handgrip strength and chair-stand performance with motoric cognitive risk syndrome in older adults
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Motor dysfunction is associated with cognitive vulnerability, but whether impairments across body regions jointly contribute to motoric cognitive risk syndrome (MCR) remains unclear. We examined the independent and joint associations of handgrip strength and chair-stand test (CST) with MCR.  This cross-sectional study included 6258 dementia-free older adults (mean age 71.5 ± 6.6 years; 63.1% women) from a community-based cohort. Handgrip strength and CST performance were used to define upper- and lower-extremity motor impairment. Participants were classified as normal, handgrip weakness only, CST impairment only, or combined motor impairment. Multivariable logistic regression was performed with adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, and clinical factors. Additive and multiplicative interactions were assessed.  MCR was present in 10.4% of participants. Using the A/B CST cutoff as the primary definition, adjusted odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) for MCR, compared with normal function, were 1.84 (1.14–2.97) for handgrip weakness only, 4.17 (2.97–5.85) for CST impairment only, and 9.17 (6.56–12.81) for combined motor impairment. Associations were directionally consistent across alternative CST cutoffs. A positive additive interaction was observed at the A/B CST cutoff (relative excess risk due to interaction = 3.48; attributable proportion = 0.40; and synergy index = 1.83), whereas multiplicative interaction was not positive.  Combined handgrip weakness and poorer CST performance were strongly associated with prevalent MCR. A positive additive interaction at the primary CST cutoff suggests that joint motor impairment may help characterize MCR-related vulnerability in older adults.

records.title: Family Decision-Making Exclusion, Widowhood, and Depressive Symptoms Among Co-Resident Older Adults in India
records.abstract: : Family co-residence is often considered protective for older adults in India but may not ensure inclusion in household decisions. This study examined how widowhood and decision-making exclusion are jointly associated with depressive symptoms among co-resident older adults. : Data came from LASI Wave 1 (2017–18) and included 27,840 married or widowed adults aged 60+. Survey-weighted logistic regression examined widowhood, decision-making exclusion, their interaction, dose-response patterns, and sex-stratified associations with CES-D depressive symptoms. : Decision-making exclusion was highest among widowed women and lowest among married men. More extensive exclusion was associated with higher depressive symptoms, while widowhood without exclusion was not significant after full adjustment. There was little evidence that widowhood and exclusion interacted. Associations with depressive symptoms were more clearly observed among women than men. : Among co-resident older adults, having a meaningful voice in family decisions may be important for mental health beyond shared residence alone.

records.title: Spousal Discrepancy in Perceived Importance of Care Needs Among Couples Managing Early-Stage Alzheimer’s Disease
records.abstract: This study examined discrepancies between persons living with dementia (PLWD) and their spousal caregivers in the perceived importance of PLWD’s care needs, and how caregivers’ dementia knowledge and empathy were associated with these discrepancies. Data were drawn from 65 couples managing early-stage Alzheimer’s disease. PLWD self-reported the importance of their physical, psychological, and social needs, while caregivers provided proxy ratings. PLWD perceived addressing their physical needs as more important than did their caregivers, whereas both partners agreed on the importance of psychological and social needs. Caregivers’ greater empathic concern was associated with smaller discrepancies in the perceived importance of physical needs; greater personal distress was associated with smaller discrepancies in social needs. Caregivers’ dementia knowledge was positively associated with discrepancies in psychological needs only when relationship quality was lower. These findings highlight the importance of caregivers’ emotional responsiveness and relational dynamics in caregiver interventions, expanding the focus beyond dementia knowledge.

records.title: Sexuality and Glycosylated Hemoglobin Levels in Partnered Older Adults With Diabetes
records.abstract: We examined associations between sexual activity, sexual quality, and glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels among partnered older adults with diabetes. Using longitudinal data from the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project, we studied 620 partnered respondents with diabetes aged 57 to 85 at baseline. We estimated mixed-effects models of sexual activity, frequency, and quality on HbA1c trajectories over ten years, including tests for gender differences.  indicated that being sexually active and having sex a few times a month were associated with more favorable HbA1c trajectories compared to being sexually inactive. Emotional satisfaction was associated with worsening HbA1c trajectories for women but stable trajectories for men. Physical pleasure showed no gender differences. The findings suggest that partnered sexuality is a meaningful, gendered aspect of older adults’ metabolic health that deserves greater attention as a dimension of diabetes care in later life.

records.title: Double Scaffold of Retirement on Subsequent Health: Revisiting Spatio-Temporality and Finance Through the Feature-Wide Effect Heterogeneity
records.abstract: This study investigates how retirement’s effect on subsequent health varies by individual attributes and their interaction. Instead of spotlighting heterogeneity for a specific, theoretically predetermined feature, I consider the feature-wide effect heterogeneity to find possible data-driven candidates that generate this heterogeneity. To accomplish this, I use causal forests and harmonized data from the Gateway to Global Aging Data (the Gateway). The  show that temporal dimensions (such as age and birth cohort) and financial dimensions (such as income and wealth) are the most important features in heterogenizing retirement’s effect on health. Based on these findings, I suggest the “double scaffold” model to comprehensively explain feature-wide effect heterogeneity.

records.title: The palliative care needs of people with multiple long-term conditions and their family caregivers: a scoping review of mixed study designs
records.abstract: As populations age, most deaths occur in people with multiple long-term conditions (MLTC). When decline is driven by coexisting conditions, the palliative phase and associated needs often go unrecognised. Improving palliative care for this group is an international priority, yet no recent review has described their needs at the end of life.  To map the extent, range and nature of evidence on the palliative care needs of people with MLTC and their family caregivers, describe its characteristics and identify knowledge gaps. Design Scoping review of quantitative, qualitative and mixed- primary studies. Eligibility criteria Adults aged ≥50 years with ≥2 long-term conditions plus indicators of advanced disease or poor prognosis. Single-condition studies, early-stage MLTC, non-disaggregated data, disease-modifying interventions and non-primary research were excluded. Sources of Evidence MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Scopus and PsycINFO, searched from inception to 8 September 2025. Charting  Records were dual-screened and charted by design, setting and established conceptual frameworks of domains of need.  Of 7568 records, 90 studies were included. Four domains were identified: (i) comprehensive support needs in the context of functional decline; (ii) proactive care needs shaped by limited death literacy and prognostic uncertainty; (iii) systems-level needs for coordination and collaboration; and (iv) compounded needs arising from inequality (diagnostic/sociodemographic).  Older adults with MLTC face complex, often unmet needs, requiring support for functional decline, equitable proactive care, coordinated systems and improved death literacy. Palliative care must be integrated, responsive to MLTC realities and guided by what matters most to patients and caregivers.

records.title: Attitudes of people living with dementia and their carers towards the use of generative artificial intelligence to inform structured medication reviews
records.abstract: Polypharmacy is common in people living with dementia (PLwD) and associated with adverse outcomes. Although Structured Medication Reviews (SMRs) are recommended to optimise medication regimens, their delivery is often constrained by limited resources. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support SMRs, yet little is known about how it is perceived by PLwD and their carers. This study explored their experiences of polypharmacy, views on SMRs and attitudes towards use of AI tools in SMRs.  Semi-structured interviews with 12 PLwD experiencing polypharmacy and two focus groups with 14 carers were conducted via Microsoft Teams or telephone and analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis.  Two themes were constructed: participants’ perspectives on meaningful SMRs, and embracing AI while preserving patient safety and the human touch. Participants described challenges in managing polypharmacy, with carers playing a central role in supporting adherence and monitoring side effects. Experiences of SMRs varied. SMRs were most valued when clinicians were empathetic and able to offer personalised guidance. Participants viewed AI use in SMRs positively, provided that such tools were well validated and used to assist rather than replace healthcare professionals. AI was also seen as potentially reducing administrative burden and supporting more person-centred care. However, some had concerns regarding patient safety and data security, highlighting the need for appropriate regulation and human oversight.  Participants were supportive of AI use in SMRs, despite concerns about safety, data security and disclosure of AI use, and emphasised the importance of patient-clinician interactions and lived experience involvement in AI tool development.

records.title: Implementing a Belgian program to enhance the uptake and effectiveness of a multifactorial falls prevention intervention in community-dwelling older adults: A mixed-methods process and implementation evaluation
records.abstract: To improve the implementation and uptake of a multifactorial falls prevention intervention, the Belgian Program to Enhance the Uptake and Effectiveness of a Multifactorial Falls Prevention Intervention in Community-Dwelling Older people (BE-EMPOWERed) program was systematically developed. It includes a 7-week group program for older people, workshops for healthcare professionals and an implementation plan with implementation guidance for primary care areas (PCAs) in Flanders. This study implemented BE-EMPOWERed in four PCAs and evaluated its implementation processes and implementation outcomes.  This embedded mixed- process evaluation was conducted over a 2-year period in four PCAs. Implementation processes and outcomes were assessed using participant lists, fidelity checklists, observations, focus group interviews and self-reported intervention costs. The process evaluation was guided by the Medical Research Council framework. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively and qualitative data were analysed using the Qualitative Analysis Guide of Leuven.  A total of 196 people participated in the group program with high attendance across sessions. Fidelity assessments across 20 group programs demonstrated high adherence to many structural and delivery-related program components. However, lower fidelity was observed for some behaviour change components. Qualitative findings suggested increased knowledge and awareness among older people, with reported application of falls prevention interventions in daily life. Overall, the findings indicate that strong engagement stemmed from group dynamics and the way group leaders delivered the program, while sustainability was hindered by limited resources and reliance on local champions.  The BE-EMPOWERed program was feasible and acceptable across diverse PCAs, with high engagement and overall good fidelity. However, challenges in sustainability highlight the need for structural support to enable long-term implementation. Study protocol ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06105437).

records.title: Prevalence of polypharmacy and potentially inappropriate prescribing in older adults with a prognosis of 6 months or less: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.abstract: Polypharmacy and potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) are common in older adults, but the prevalence in those with a prognosis of 6 months or less is poorly characterised. We estimated the prevalence of polypharmacy, PIMs and potential prescribing omissions (PPOs) in older adults approaching end of life.  We systematically searched six databases from inception to 30 April 2026, for studies reporting polypharmacy (≥5 medications) or PIMs in adults aged ≥65 years with life-limiting illnesses (≤6-month prognosis). Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data and assessed bias using Joanna Briggs Institute or Newcastle-Ottawa tools. Pooled prevalence used random-effects models. Heterogeneity was explored by setting, region and assessment tool. The review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023454636). Findings Eighteen studies (499 853 participants, 52.3% female) were included in this review. Pooled prevalence of polypharmacy was 76% (95% CI 65%–87%) with excessive polypharmacy (≥10 medications) at 34% (9%–58%). PIM prevalence was high at 54% (40%–68%), and remained above 50% until the final week of life, with preventive medications (statins, antithrombotics, proton pump inhibitors) often continued until death. Substantial heterogeneity was present in all pooled analyses (I2 > 99%), highlighting considerable variability across studies. Only two studies assessed PPOs 30% lacked prophylactic laxatives with opioids while 76.6% lacked strong opioids for moderate–severe cancer pain. Interpretation Polypharmacy and PIMs use are highly prevalent among people with limited life prognosis, suggesting that evidence-based deprescribing protocols are needed for this vulnerable population. Nevertheless, this needs to be taken in light of the substantial heterogeneity of PIM definitions, underscoring the need for standardised PIM assessment in this population.

records.title: The trajectories of comprehensive capacity of bedridden older people based on latent growth mixture models: a longitudinal study
records.abstract: Bedridden older people generally have poor comprehensive capacity and are prone to multi-system complications including pressure injuries and lower limb venous thrombosis, imposing heavy caregiving and financial burdens and severely affecting their health.  To identify distinct trajectories of ability in bedridden older people and characteristics distinguishing the trajectories, while assessing the prognostic value of these trajectories for early risk identification of pressure injury and deep-vein thrombosis (DVT). Participants Two hundred twenty six bedridden older people aged 65 years and above from two nursing homes in China.  Patients were required 5 assessments during 1-year follow-up period. Latent Growth Mixture Modelling identified distinct trajectories, multinomial logistic regression identified characteristics distinguishing the trajectories and generalised estimating equations evaluated associations between trajectories and pressure injury and DVT.  There are three distinct trajectories of comprehensive capacity among bedridden older people, including severe impairment with stable type (63.5%); moderate impairment with slowly deteriorating type (16.3%); moderate-to-severe impairment with fluctuating type (20.2%). Characteristics distinguishing the trajectories were tooth loss, hypertension, indwelling gastric tube and dysphagia. Compared with the severe impairment stable type, the other two groups had higher pressure injury risk; the moderate impairment with slowly deteriorating type also had higher DVT risk.  Capacity trajectories of bedridden older people are heterogeneous. Nurses may want to focus on those with tooth loss, hypertension, indwelling gastric tube and dysphagia to deliver targeted care. These trajectories are significantly associated with pressure injury and deep vein thrombosis risks. Their identification enables earlier risk stratification and more targeted prevention.

records.title: Association of muscle strength with the incidence of venous thromboembolism and all-cause mortality among patients: a prospective cohort study
records.abstract: Muscle strength is a well-established indicator of overall health, yet its prospective association with the incidence and prognosis of venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains inconsistent.  This prospective cohort study included 481 945 participants without prior VTE from the UK Biobank for incidence analysis, and 14 908 patients with prevalent VTE at baseline for prognostic analysis. Muscle strength was assessed using grip strength relative to body weight and categorised into sex- and age-specific tertiles. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for incident VTE and all-cause mortality.  Over a median follow-up of 13.72 years, 15 774 incident VTE events were documented. Each 1-standard deviation increase in muscle strength was associated with a 13% reduction in VTE risk (HR 0.87, 95% CI: 0.85–0.89). Compared with the low muscle strength group, participants in the middle and high tertiles had 12% (HR 0.88, 95% CI: 0.84–0.92) and 19% (HR 0.81, 95% CI: 0.77–0.84) lower risk of VTE. This inverse association remained consistent across all genetic risk strata. Among patients with VTE, 2884 deaths occurred during follow-up. Each 1-standard deviation increase was associated with a 14% lower mortality risk (HR 0.86, 95% CI: 0.82–0.90). High and middle muscle strength were associated with 21% (HR 0.79, 95% CI: 0.72–0.87) and 17% (HR 0.83, 95% CI: 0.76–0.91) lower all-cause mortality versus low strength.  Higher muscle strength is associated with a lower risk of incident VTE, regardless of genetic predisposition, and with lower mortality among patients with VTE.

records.title: Associations between income support payments and entry to long-term care facilities: a national retrospective cohort study
records.abstract: To examine associations between amount of income support received and entry into long-term care facilities (LTCFs) among older income support recipients, by homeownership status.  A national retrospective cohort study was conducted. Individuals aged 65–105 years who received income support and had a first-time long-term care eligibility assessment in Australia between 01/01/2010 and 30/06/2021 were included. Associations between means-tested income support payments and rate of entry into LTCFs stratified by homeownership status were assessed using inverse probability of treatment weighted, cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models. Additional analyses included sex-specific analyses and sub-group analyses to examine associations for people with dementia.  In total, 633 253 people were included [56.2% (n = 355 917) female; median age 82 years (interquartile range 76–86); 17.8% (n = 112 724) living with dementia; 69.1% (n = 437 445) homeowners]. Higher levels of income support were associated with a higher rate of entry into LTCFs for both homeowners [hazard ratio (HR) highest quartile vs lowest quartile: 1.08; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.06–1.10] and non-homeowners [HR 1.08; 95% CI 1.05–1.12]. Findings were consistent for males, but for females, only those with moderate income support (third quartile) had a higher rate of LTCF entry. The findings were similar when only including people with dementia.  Greater reliance on means-tested income support payments, a potential indicator of financial vulnerability in later life, was associated with a higher rate of entry into LTCFs among both homeowners and non-homeowners. The study findings also suggest a complex relationship between income support reliance later in life and LTCF entry among older females.

records.title: Mixed-method process evaluation of the Evidence-based Medication knowledge Brokers in Residential Aged CarE (EMBRACE) helix–counterbalanced randomised controlled trial
records.abstract: Effective implementation of guidelines into residential aged care facilities (RACFs) is important for high-quality care. The 12-month Evidence-based Medication knowledge Brokers in Residential Aged CarE (EMBRACE) helix–counterbalanced randomised controlled trial evaluated three strategies to implement Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Appropriate Use of Psychotropic Medications in People Living with Dementia and in Residential Aged Care: (i) passive distribution of Guideline material, (ii) pharmacist-led staff education and (iii) knowledge broker-led Guideline implementation. All three strategies reduced Guideline non-concordance over time, with no significant difference between strategies. This mixed-method process evaluation examined delivery of the implementation strategies, including contextual factors important for Guideline implementation.  Semi-structured interviews conducted with 34 health and care professionals at 12 months were thematically analysed using a deductive approach informed by the Grant framework. Descriptive statistics summarised quantitative data from a post-trial survey completed by intervention pharmacists.  Distribution of Guideline materials occurred opportunistically with RACF staff preferring summary materials (e.g. one-page factsheets). Pharmacist-led staff education was tailored to be shorter, more frequent and delivered one-on-one or in small groups. Knowledge broker pharmacists spent a median 70% of time delivering quality improvement activities including audit and feedback and integrating psychotropic best practice into RACF procedures and digital systems. Facilitators of successful Guideline implementation included early engagement with aged care leadership and knowledge broker integration into the team.  Guideline implementation efforts in RACFs may benefit from a multifaceted implementation approach involving early engagement with aged care leadership and contextualised delivery of implementation strategies according to staff preferences and needs.

records.title: New horizons in adaptive capacity and heat-related health in older people: integrating frailty, energy insecurity and social resources
records.abstract: Extreme heat is a major environmental threat to healthy ageing, with older people experiencing the highest rates of heat-related morbidity and mortality. Although age-related physiological changes, multimorbidity and frailty remain key determinants of heat susceptibility, climate change, social inequalities and energy insecurity are reshaping the conditions in which older people experience and respond to thermal stress. This narrative New Horizons review integrates evidence identified through a structured, non-systematic search of peer-reviewed literature and relevant institutional reports across geriatric medicine, environmental health and climate science. It examines how frailty, intrinsic capacity, housing, energy affordability and social frailty influence the ability of older people to recognise risk, access protection and respond effectively to extreme heat. Particular attention is given to energy insecurity and summer cooling poverty, through which limited access to affordable household energy may undermine resilience. Ageing models primarily characterise individual vulnerability and functioning within the environment, whereas climate vulnerability models organise risk around exposure, sensitivity and adaptation; we use adaptive capacity to connect these perspectives by asking whether personal and contextual resources can be mobilised for protection. It may provide a conceptual basis for developing and subsequently validating a heat-adapted comprehensive geriatric assessment and for informing targeted prevention and climate adaptation policies for ageing populations.

records.title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial
records.abstract: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown.  In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise.  EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: −10.9%, 95%CI: −21.4;−0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: −9.80, 95%CI: −18.3;−1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis.  n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.

records.title: The experience of family caregivers when their loved one is home hospitalized: a mixed methods analysis of a randomized controlled trial
records.abstract: Home hospital has been shown to achieve comparable, if not better, clinical and patient-centred outcomes compared to brick-and-mortar (BAM) hospitalisation. Family caregivers (FCs) play an essential role in delivering home hospital care; however, their perceptions towards the home hospital model remain an active area of inquiry, particularly in rural settings.  We conducted a mixed  analysis of FCs of patients participating in a multicenter randomised controlled trial of rural home hospital in the USA and Canada. We compared pre- and post-intervention burden among home hospital and BAM caregivers with the Zarit Burden Interview-12 (ZBI-12) scale (n = 20 home hospital, n = 10 BAM). We conducted semi-structured qualitative interviews with home hospital caregivers (n = 19). Qualitative data were coded and analysed using thematic analysis to construct core themes and subthemes.  There was no significant difference in median ZBI-12 scores between home hospital and BAM at admission (4 interquartile range [IQR 2–9.3] vs 5 [IQR 0.3–9.3]; P = .723), discharge (6 [3.3–8] vs 7.5 [2.5–11.8], P = .309), or change from admission to discharge (0 [−2.5 to 3] vs 1.5 [0–3.5]; P = .269). Our qualitative analysis revealed three central themes: (i) The caregiving experience was positively shaped by strong communication and shared decision-making with the care team; (ii) Caregivers described receiving high-quality home hospital care, particularly surrounding patient-centeredness and technology; and (iii) Home hospital was perceived to offer greater flexibility, comfort and psychosocial support compared to BAM hospitalisation.  Home hospital provides numerous benefits for FCs without increasing perceived burden; further work is needed to establish potential supports to optimise their experience.

records.title: Profiling perceived knowledge, relevance and interest across geriatric topics of health and social care professionals: multinational electronic cross-sectional survey
records.abstract: Interprofessional training is essential for high-quality care of older adults. Despite widespread recognition of its importance, evidence on perceived geriatric competence remains limited to studies on single countries or professions.  Secondary analysis of a COST Action multinational multilingual web-based survey (PROmoting GeRiAtric Medicine in countries where it is still eMergING, PROGRAMMING) conducted across the 27 European Union Member States (EU-27) and non-EU-27 countries between 9 October 2023 and 5 June 2024. Four thousand seven hundred eighty-eight professionals from 10 core health and social care groups were included. We explored perceived Knowledge, Relevance and Interest across seven domains required for comprehensive geriatric assessment: frailty, falls and mobility, delirium, depression, mild cognitive impairment and dementia screening, nutritional assessment and malnutrition, polypharmacy and deprescribing. Student’s t test; one-way analysis of variance, hierarchical clustering and latent class analysis were used to identify interprofessional differences and shared patterns across professions.  Mean age was 42.4 years (SD 11.9); 3432 (71.7%) were women; 2893 (60.4%) worked in EU-27 countries. Interprofessional differences were observed across all topics. Physiotherapists led in falls and mobility (mean 4.21, SD 0.75), pharmacists in polypharmacy and deprescribing (mean 3.51, SD 1.07), and psychologists/psychotherapists in depression (mean 3.96, SD 0.82). A medical doctors–nurses–pharmacists cluster emerged for Knowledge and Interest; 34.4% pharmacists fell in the low relevance class. Social workers and speech and language therapists showed a low Knowledge–high Interest mismatch. EU-27 professionals reported higher scores than non-EU-27 professionals across most topics (P  Perceived knowledge, relevance and interest showed substantial variation across professions and regions, while revealing shared professional profiles. This may inform team-based interprofessional education.

records.title: Invasive versus conservative strategy for older patients with myocardial infarction based on cognitive function: the SENIOR-RITA cognition analysis
records.abstract: Older adults with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and cognitive impairment experience higher cardiovascular risk than patients with normal cognition. It remains unclear how cognition should influence whether older adults receive an invasive or conservative treatment strategy.  To compare an invasive and conservative treatment strategy among older adults with NSTEMI and cognitive impairment.  This study is a pre-specified analysis of the SENIOR-RITA randomised controlled trial. Cognition was measured at randomisation using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Patients were followed up for a median of 4.1 years postrandomisation. The primary outcome was a composite of time to cardiovascular death or nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI).  MoCA was available for 1455 patients (95.8%) who underwent randomisation. Within the cognitively impaired group (909 patients), the primary outcome occurred in 116 patients (26.8%) in the invasive group and in 141 patients (29.6%) in the conservative group (hazard ratio [HR], 0.85; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 1.10; P = 0.20). Nonfatal MI occurred in 48 patients (11.1%) in the invasive group and in 75 patients (15.8%) in the conservative group (HR 0.64; 95% CI, 0.44 to 0.92). However, there was no interaction between treatment strategy and cognition.  Among those with evidence of cognitive impairment at randomisation, an invasive treatment strategy did not reduce the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death or nonfatal MI, and there was no evidence of treatment effect heterogeneity based on cognition. The reduction in nonfatal MI events among those with cognitive impairment should be interpreted as an exploratory finding.

records.title: Social Engagement and Cognitive Function Among Chinese Older Adults During the COVID-19 Outbreak: Gender and Urban–Rural Disparities
records.abstract: This study examines the association between reduced social engagement and cognitive function among older adults in China during the COVID-19 pandemic with a focus on gender and urban–rural differences.  Using China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study data, we used OLS regression to assess changes in cognitive function before and during the pandemic and their associations with changes in physical and cognitively stimulating activities.  Cognitive function declined across social groups, with the largest decline among urban women. Moderate physical activity was not associated with less cognitive function, whereas decreased engagement in cognitively stimulating activities was associated with greater decline.  Forms of social engagement were associated with cognitive function of older adults in distinct ways, underscoring the need for a nuanced rather than uniform interpretation. The observed differences in cognitive function by subgroups suggest a need for targeted interventions to support older populations in the post-pandemic context.

records.title: Exploring Quality of Life Through Residents’ Voice in Nursing Homes: A Qualitative Study of a Montessori-Based Person-Centered Model of Care
records.abstract: Person-centered care (PCC) is the gold standard for improving the quality of life (QoL) of people living with dementia. The Montessori method represents a practical model for implementing PCC in Nursing Homes (NHs). To date, no study has documented how residents describe their QoL in NHs implementing this method using a self-report approach consistent with PCC principles. This study explores residents’ perceptions of their QoL, as well as how they relate it to the care model, using a qualitative self-assessment tool. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twenty-nine residents from two NHs with high levels of Montessori implementation assessed using a validated tool. All interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three interconnected themes emerged. The first examines the components of QoL that matter most to residents. The second explores how the care model influences these determinants. Finally, the third describes residents’ self-assessment of QoL shaped by individual factors. Our study contributes to a better understanding of the Montessori method as a comprehensive PCC model from residents’ perspectives and deepens knowledge of the extent to which it can shape their QoL. These findings also provide practical and methodological insights for evaluating QoL and guiding care models promoting QoL.

records.title: Senescence Biomarkers Predict Physical Function and Clinical Outcomes After Heart Failure Hospitalization: Insights From REHAB-HF
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) is the most common cause of hospitalization in older adults. Cellular senescence, a hallmark of aging biology, has been implicated in heart failure pathophysiology and functional decline via the pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). We evaluated the association between SASP and physical function in older adults hospitalized for ADHF.  REHAB-HF was a trial of older adults hospitalized for ADHF randomized to a novel physical rehabilitation intervention or attention control. We measured a panel of 18-SASP analytes at in-hospital baseline and at 3-month follow-up. Outcomes included short physical performance battery (SPPB) and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD). Statistical analysis included principal component analysis (PCA) of log- and z-transformed SASP values. Associations were evaluated with multivariable regression models adjusted for age, sex, and intervention arm.  Samples were available for 226 (65%) of the REHAB-HF participants with mean age (SD) 72.3 (8), 53% female, 52% HFpEF, and 53% assigned to rehab intervention. Principal Component 1 (PC1) reflected a coordinated signal across biomarkers of inflammation and immune signaling. PC1 was associated with poorer function at baseline [(SPPB -0.46 [-0.77, -0.14]; p = 0.004 and 6MWD -19.7 meters [-32.7, -6.7]; p = 0.003)]. Increasing SASP over time was associated with clinically significant reduced physical function improvement (ΔSPPB -1.80 [-2.58, -1.03]; p  Higher SASP levels were associated with poorer physical function recovery in older patients hospitalized for ADHF. These findings suggest that inflammatory SASP biomarkers may improve risk stratification and potentially guide therapeutic strategies. REHAB-HF trial is registered at clinicaltrials.gov Clinical Trial Registry NCT02196038

records.title: Intervention-Type-Specific Effects on Healthy Aging of Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
records.abstract: and  Healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment requires preserving physical, cognitive, and psychosocial functioning to sustain their independence and quality of life. However, existing interventions vary in design, delivery format, and composition, and evidence regarding their effectiveness across these three core domains remains inconsistent. This study aimed to identify the most effective intervention types for specific domains of healthy aging. Research Design and  Five electronic databases were searched for studies published from October 2015 to June 2026. Randomized controlled trials reporting at least two outcomes—among physical capability, cognitive function, or psychosocial well-being—were reviewed. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 tool. A dependency-aware multilevel random-effects meta-analysis with trial-clustered robust inference was conducted in R, supplemented by moderator tests, prediction intervals, sensitivity analyses, reporting-bias assessments, and GRADE evaluations.  Multicomponent interventions were associated with beneficial effects on cognitive and psychosocial outcomes, whereas group-based interventions showed beneficial effects across all three domains and a significantly greater effect on cognitive function than individually delivered interventions. Despite substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals, these findings were generally robust across sensitivity analyses.  The observed advantages of group-based delivery, particularly for cognitive function, and multicomponent approaches for cognitive and psychosocial outcomes highlight the domain-specific nature of intervention effects. These findings support tailoring intervention delivery and component configuration to the targeted domain rather than applying a uniform approach to healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment.

records.title: Perceptions, Knowledge, and Adaptive actions in Response to Climate Events: A Scoping Review of Climate Health Literacy among Community Dwelling Older Adults
records.abstract: and  Extreme climate events can threaten older adults’ health. The purpose of this study was to summarize existing literature on older adults’ climate health literacy, defined as their ability to find and access, understand, and act upon information related to climate-related health threats. Research Design and  A scoping review was conducted in the bibliographic databases Embase, Medline and Scopus and grey literature sources Cornell Initiative for Research on Climate and Aging and Climate Change and Human Health Literature portals with searches updated January 2026. English language studies of community-dwelling adults aged 60 years and older were included if they reported at least one aspect of climate health literacy. Quantitative data were reported as median percentages, and qualitative themes were categorized.  Fifty-nine studies, including 22,992 records for 20,296 unique participants, were included. Most recognized the health risks of extreme climate events but did not identify personal vulnerability. Television was the most cited source of information and hydration, clothing and environment modification, and activity adjustment were the most utilized adaptive actions. Barriers to adaptive actions included financial constraints, limited mobility and lack of supports. The effectiveness of studied interventions was mixed, influenced by intervention type and study design.  Despite access to information and awareness of climate-related health threats, gaps remain in personal risk perception and translation of knowledge into actions. Improving climate health literacy among older adults requires public health messaging, engagement of trustworthy authorities, and interventions addressing social and structural barriers.

records.title: Adaptive driving, not unsafe: Older drivers’ compensatory strategies and lower simulated crash risk
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: The global aging population has led to an increasing number of older active drivers. While age-related physical and cognitive changes are associated with increased crash risk, specific on-road adaptations and safety outcomes of older drivers remain unclear. This study examined distinct driving characteristics, personality traits, and cognitive processes related to decision-making among middle-aged and older drivers in a simulated driving environment.  We assessed driving performance in a high-fidelity motorcycle simulator across drivers in three age groups: middle-aged (30-54; n = 40), aged 65–74 (n = 34), and aged 75 + (75-86; n = 29). Comparative analysis focused on speed regulation, braking behavior, control stability, and accident rates. Additionally, questionnaire measures and a computerized decision-making task were employed to assess risk perception and risky decision-making.  Compared to the middle-aged group, both older groups demonstrated a significantly more conservative driving profile: lower mean speeds, fewer speeding violations, longer braking maneuvers, reduced variation in throttle control, and a lower incidence of simulated accidents. Drivers aged 75+ also reported higher perceived risk in driving scenarios and displayed diminished discrimination between risk and non-risk situations in a braking decision task. Mediation analyses showed that steering variance in the simulator and self-reported health/safety risk-taking significantly mediated the relationship between age group and number of accidents. Discussion The findings indicate that older drivers adopt proactive compensatory strategies that could result in fewer simulated accidents. These findings challenge a purely deficit-oriented perspective on older driver safety, underscoring the critical role of behavioral adaptation and strategic self-regulation in maintaining safe mobility.

records.title: Living Alone With Dementia: Managing Without Informal Support to Contact and Navigate Services
records.abstract: Purpose: People with dementia can and do live successfully on their own, but there are additional challenges for people living alone without informal support. This paper reports findings of the first study in the UK to examine needs and experiences of, and services for, people with dementia who live alone without informal support. Method: The study involved a service audit of 13 local authority commissioners in two English regions, interviews with 22 people with dementia who live alone without informal carers, and case studies of four services supporting this group. Findings: Awareness of this population among commissioners was limited. There were very few services which explicitly supported this group, and some mainstream services excluded people without carers. None of the local authorities collected data on numbers of people with dementia living alone, or those without informal support, in their area. Some participants with dementia had contacted social care, but this had not always resulted in appropriate support, and people reported problematic interactions with staff, assumptions that friends would provide care, and support not being available at the right time. Self-funders were left with little support. People with dementia were resourceful, using general services, technology, and other tactics, including cleaners, meal delivery, community taxis, and automatic reminders to organise their lives. However, as many of these additional services have a cost attached, there is potential to exacerbate existing inequalities. Participants wanted more support, particularly with finances and administrative tasks. Services can help this group with supported handovers, allowing self-referral back into a service, and keeping case files open. : Both the number of people with dementia, and the number of people ageing without children, are rising, and it will therefore become increasingly important to facilitate effective support for people with dementia to live independently without informal support.

records.title: Delirium Occurrence and Associated Factors Among Patients With Dementia and Mild Cognitive Impairment Admitted to Long-Term Care Hospitals: Cross-Sectional Study
records.abstract: Delirium is common among older adults, particularly those with cognitive impairment. However, delirium among patients with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in long-term care (LTC) hospitals has received limited attention.  This study aimed to examine delirium occurrence and associated factors among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals.  This cross-sectional study included 142 patients aged 65 years or older with dementia (n=100, 70.4%) or MCI (n=42, 29.6%) at 2 LTC hospitals in South Korea between September 2021 and August 2022. Delirium occurrence was defined as at least 1 positive Short Confusion Assessment Method assessment during twice-daily assessments over 4 weeks, including the first assessment. Multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors overall and within each cognitive group.  Delirium was identified in 55 (38.7%) of 142 patients. The proportion was 41% (41/100) in patients with dementia and 33.3% (14/42) in patients with MCI. Hypoactive delirium was the most common subtype (33/55, 60%). Overall, female sex (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 4.344, 95% CI 1.794-10.515; P=.001), immobility (aOR 4.953, 95% CI 1.857-13.205; P=.001), and analgesic use (aOR 3.641, 95% CI 1.262-10.501; P=.02) were associated with delirium. Infection was inversely associated with delirium (aOR 0.251, 95% CI 0.101-0.623; P=.003). In patients with dementia, female sex, immobility, analgesic use, and pain were associated with delirium. Diaper use was associated with delirium in patients with MCI.  Delirium was common among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals. The findings support regular delirium assessment, with attention to mobility and pain-related care needs. Further studies are needed to clarify the factors associated with delirium in each cognitive group.

records.title: Telemonitoring Adoption Among Older Adults: Sequential Mixed Methods Study of Message Framing and Structural Influence
records.abstract: Telemonitoring offers solutions for remote health management among older adults; yet, acceptance varies based on individual perceptions and presentation strategies.  This 2-phased sequential mixed  study examines the role of message framing on telemonitoring adoption among low-income older adults.  Phase 1 involved in-depth interviews with 17 older adults, identifying key facilitators (accessibility, affordability, and health benefits) and barriers (preference for in-person consultations, technological limitations, and information processing difficulties) of telemonitoring. Building on these insights, phase 2 used an experimental study with 120 participants assessing message framing effects (episodic vs thematic) and modalities (video vs photo-text) on telemonitoring adoption.  Episodic framing did not produce a significant main effect on attitudes toward telemonitoring; however, its effect was moderated by external locus of control (LOC), with episodic framing associated with more positive attitudes among participants lower in external LOC, and thematic framing more favorable among those higher in external LOC.  Convenience, cost, and health benefits emerged as key adoption drivers, while traditional consultation preferences and cognitive processing challenges posed barriers. Theoretical and practical implications were discussed.

records.title: A Longitudinal Study on Social Isolation, Chronic Diseases, and Depressive Symptoms: Evidence From the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging
records.abstract: This study examined the longitudinal effects of social isolation on chronic diseases and depressive symptoms among middle-aged and older adults in South Korea, with attention to gender and age differences. Method Using data from three waves of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging, longitudinal path analysis was conducted on 5,585 participants.  Women and older adults showed higher levels of social isolation, chronic diseases, and depressive symptoms, indicating greater vulnerability. Significant longitudinal and bidirectional associations emerged among social isolation, chronic diseases, and depressive symptoms over time. While gender differences in long-term patterns were modest, age-related disparities were more substantial.  These findings underscore the importance of strengthening community-based social networks and implementing both conventional outreach—such as home visits—and innovative approaches, including technology-assisted companionship, to identify socially isolated individuals, particularly older adults.

records.title: I Did It My Way Theatre: Research and Live Theatre as Applied to the Transition of Relocating Older Adults
records.abstract: Relocation is an option for older adults who leave their home to improve their emotional well-being, physical health, and safety. Moves can enhance agency or foster a loss of empowerment. We explored older adults’ transition experiences from a community setting to a retirement community and created messaging to help with experiences of older adults and their self-identified family or friend caregivers. We conducted 30 telephone interviews and analyzed relocation experiences, which informed I Did It My Way Theatre. The theatrical presentation was performed for over 100 older adult residents and caregivers. Our goal was to ease the transition experiences by disseminating findings to those involved in similar relocation situations. Attendees completed a post-performance questionnaire asking how the play helped them understand relocation and held table discussions concerning production themes. Follow-up interviews with 11 participants revealed that the play delivered hard messages in an impactful way.

records.title: Dementia Knowledge Among Older Asian Americans: Roles of Digital Literacy, Planning Attitudes, and Sociocultural Contexts
records.abstract: Knowledge of dementia facilitates early detection, care planning, and stigma reduction, yet less is known about dementia knowledge among Asian American populations. This study examined correlates of dementia knowledge among 505 Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese Americans aged 50 and older residing in Central Florida. Dementia knowledge was assessed using the Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale with four subscales. Linear regression analyses examined associations of dementia knowledge with sociodemographic, immigration, social, digital and information, and dementia experiences and attitudinal factors. Participants demonstrated low overall dementia knowledge. Digital literacy was positively associated with total dementia knowledge and all subscales except communication and behavior. Limited English proficiency was negatively associated with knowledge in the causes and characteristics subscale. The perceived importance of dementia planning was positively associated with total dementia knowledge and three subscales. Subscale-specific findings should be interpreted cautiously because of varying subscale reliability, particularly for communication and behavior.

records.title: Third Places, Walkable Access, and Neighborhood Satisfaction Among Older Adults
records.abstract: Neighborhood satisfaction is a key indicator of well-being and community quality of life, yet its relationship with third place engagement remains underexplored.  This study examines how third place engagement, access, and perceived built environments relate to physical livability, social connectedness, and overall neighborhood satisfaction among older adults.  Survey data were collected from 515 adults aged 65 and older in the Orlando area, and separate Ordinary Least Squares regression models were used.  The  indicate that neighborhood satisfaction is multidimensional, with shared yet distinct correlates across domains. Third place engagement and walkable access were consistently associated with all three outcomes. Socially oriented third place use was more closely tied to social connectedness, while built environment quality aligned with physical livability. Overall satisfaction reflected both domains, highlighting the value of viewing neighborhood satisfaction as related but distinct constructs shaped by functional and social experiences among older adults.

records.title: Need-Conditioned Uncertainty and Perceived Non-Provision of Community Services: Social Participation and Functional Status Among Older Adults in Urban China
records.abstract: Older adults who need community services may remain uncertain whether those services are locally provided or judge that they are not. Research on perceived unmet need often combines these positions. Using a cross-sectional survey of 929 adults aged 60 or older in urban Jiangsu, China, we paired reported need with perceived provision across 20 services and distinguished awareness gaps, perceived non-provision, and comparison uncertainty for services not reported as needed. Fractional logit models examined associations with social participation and functional status. Greater social participation was associated with fewer awareness gaps, concentrated among adults with ADL disability (−8.75 percentage points per SD). A weaker, less stable association with perceived non-provision appeared among functionally independent adults, and no counterpart appeared for comparison uncertainty. Unresolved uncertainty and negative provision judgments may call for different responses, and outreach may be especially relevant for older adults with ADL disability.

records.title: Does incident multimorbidity mediate the relationship between lifetime trauma and trajectories of cognitive function in later life?
records.abstract: and  Prior research has examined the relationship between traumatic experiences and cognitive function in adulthood. We build on this literature by using a life course perspective to ask whether incident multimorbidity mediates the relationship between lifetime trauma and trajectories of cognitive function. Research Design and  We use latent growth curve models and data from the 2010-2020 waves of the Health and Retirement Study (N = 16,662) to examine the relationship between lifetime trauma, incident multimorbidity, and the intercept and slope of cognitive function.   indicate that trauma is associated with a higher intercept of cognitive function and greater cognitive decline. Lifetime trauma is also associated with higher risk of incident multimorbidity, which, in turn, is associated with a lower intercept of cognitive function.  Incident multimorbidity has an upstream influence on poor cognitive function among people exposed to trauma. Interventions may be needed for people exposed to trauma over the life course to reduce the risk of disease and cognitive decline in later life.

records.title: Content Analysis of Free Online Information and Support Available to Young Dementia Carers Across Europe
records.abstract: The aim of this study was to gain insight into young dementia carer-specific content provided on the websites of dementia and (young) carers organizations in seven European countries including: the UK, the Netherlands, Italy, Greece, Portugal, Ireland and Sweden. Research questions were: 1). What types of young dementia carer-specific content are available on national websites of dementia and (young) carers organizations across Europe? and 2). How does the content address the complex impact that dementia can have on young dementia carers? The identification of websites was informed by the contextual characteristics of each country in relation to dementia and young carers support and services. A standard protocol describing the website inclusion and exclusion criteria, data extraction and content analysis using a categorical coding framework was followed. Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarize data within and across countries. A total of 312 organizations with active websites meeting the eligibility criteria across countries were identified, and their websites reviewed. Content relevant to young dementia carers was identified in 28% (n = 86) of the websites, with uneven availability of resources across Europe and very limited resources in some countries. Most contents addressed five categories: Diagnosis & symptoms, Uncertainty & family distress, Changes in roles, Stigma & isolation and Identifying need for support. A lack of tailored resources to support young dementia carers was identified, particularly in relation to two categories: Grief & loss and Education & life planning. Only a minority of websites included young dementia carer-specific content. These websites primarily focused on general support needs and explanations of dementia, while key areas such as guidance on school, career, and life planning remain underdeveloped. There is a need for greater recognition of young dementia carers, clearer terminology, and more developmentally appropriate and practically oriented resources to strengthen online support for these carers across Europe.

records.title: Disrupted Activities and Caregivers' Resilience and Positive Affect
records.abstract: and  Caregiving for older adults imposes substantial physical and emotional costs, yet less attention has been paid to how disruptions in personally valued activities and caregiver–care recipient relationship quality relate to caregivers’ psychological well-being over time. Drawing on the activity restriction model and conservation of resource theory, this longitudinal study examined how within-person changes in disrupted valued activities (DVA) and negative relationship quality (NRQ) influence caregivers’ resilience and positive affect. Research Design and  Data came from three waves of the National Study of Caregiving, linked to the National Health and Aging Trends Study. The analytic sample included 2,415 caregivers who provided 3,441 caregiver-wave observations, nested within 1,559 care recipients. Three-level linear mixed models decomposed DVA and NRQ into between-person and within-person components and adjusted for caregiver characteristics, care-recipient dementia status, and activities of daily living (ADL) limitations.  Resilience and positive affect showed substantial variation between-person and within-person. Higher average and higher-than-usual DVA were each associated with lower positive affect and resilience. Higher average NRQ was associated with lower positive affect and resilience, whereas higher-than-usual NRQ was associated with lower positive affect but not resilience. Care-recipient dementia status and ADL limitations were not associated with either outcome once caregiver characteristics were considered.  DVA and NRQ appear to be distinct sources of resource loss, independently linked to lower caregiver well-being across and within caregivers over time. Interventions may be effective by targeting either the maintenance of meaningful activities or improvements in relationship quality.

records.title: Yearning to Be Our Younger Self: The Relationship Between Grief and Yearning to Internalized Ageism and Ableism
records.abstract: Internalized ageist and ableist beliefs significantly influence health outcomes, happiness, and longevity. Idealization of youth and pervasive ageist and ableist narratives devalue aging, contributing to perceptions of later life and potentially fostering grief over lost opportunities. To develop evidence-based interventions, it is essential to examine the potential relationship between grief, yearning, and fears about aging. A cross-sectional survey was conducted using ResearchMatch, and 384 individuals responded to questions regarding ageism, ableism, and experiences with grief. Yearning was significantly associated with internalized ageism, excessive fear of aging, and loss of physical health. Grief was significantly associated with age, internalized ageism, and excessive fear of aging. Interventions to address feelings of loss as we age, both experienced and anticipated, can be developed to address and improve personal attitudes toward growing older.

records.title: Spiritual Reminiscence Therapy for Older Persons With Dementia: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: Spirituality is a core component of person-centred dementia care, yet spiritual needs may be under-recognised as cognition and communication decline. Spiritual Reminiscence Therapy (SRT) is a structured intervention that emphasises meaning-making and existential reflection rather than autobiographical recall alone. We examined the clinical outcomes and implementation characteristics of SRT in older adults with dementia.  A scoping review was conducted using Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. Electronic databases (Cochrane, EMBASE, MEDLINE, PubMed and PsycINFO) were searched from inception to 26 December 2025, supplemented by grey literature and reference screening. Eligible English-language quantitative and qualitative studies evaluating SRT in adults aged ≥65 years with dementia were included. Data were synthesised descriptively.  Four studies met inclusion criteria (2 qualitative, 1 randomized controlled trial, 1 prospective cohort study). SRT was associated with improvements in spiritual well-being, life meaning and hope. Psychological outcomes suggested increased life satisfaction and reduced depressive symptoms. Qualitative findings indicated enhanced social connectedness in residential care settings. Evidence for cognitive benefit was inconsistent and clinically modest, and functional outcomes were rarely assessed. Reporting of intervention delivery and implementation processes was variable.  SRT may improve meaning-related and depressive symptoms in persons with dementia, however extant evidence is limited and methodologically heterogenous. Future research prioritizing standardised outcomes, longer follow-up and formal implementation evaluation are needed before broader integration into routine psychogeriatric practice.

records.title: Epigenetic aging in people with HIV across the life course: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Epigenetic aging algorithms are emerging tools for understanding the biological effects of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). A growing body of literature has applied DNA methylation-based epigenetic clocks in people living with HIV (PWH) across the life course, examining epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) in relation to HIV infection, antiretroviral therapy (ART), comorbidities, and clinical biomarkers (e.g., viral load, CD4 T-cell counts). This systematic review (Prospero: CRD420251126874) summarizes and synthesizes the current evidence on epigenetic aging in PWH across the life course and identifies critical knowledge gaps for future research. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Medline through June 26, 2026. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and assessed studies for risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. We created a narrative synthesis of  and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA. Fifty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. More than half (n = 33) examined EAA in PWH compared to an uninfected control population. We identified heterogeneity in study populations and design, biospecimens profiled, platforms used for DNA methylation analysis, and epigenetic clocks employed. Only 6 studies included participants younger than 18 years and no studies focused exclusively on individuals over 65 years. Only 10 studies examined longitudinal changes in EAA. Thirty-seven papers evaluated associations between EAA and comorbidities. A meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA across 14 studies found a mean difference of 3.41 years (95%CI 2.22, 4.60) in PWH relative to controls. Current evidence supports accelerated EAA among PWH but highlights substantial methodological heterogeneity and important knowledge gaps. Longitudinal studies of EAA in PWH are needed in populations under 18 and over 65, to clarify the effects of ART, clinical biomarkers, and age-related comorbidities, and determine the clinical utility of epigenetic aging biomarkers.

records.title: Fear-Specific Technophobia as a Mediator Between Daily Technical Support and Instrumental Versus Hedonic Technology Use in Later Life: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
records.abstract: Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults’ digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships.  This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults’ instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender.  A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55‐86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI.  DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=−0.455, 95% BCa CI −0.632 to −0.229; P P =.12) or human-machine ambiguity ( P =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=−0.215, 95% BCa CI −0.410 to −0.009; P =.05 and β=−0.211, 95% BCa CI −0.389 to −0.001; P =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203; P =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075; P =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518; P =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI −0.002 to 0.116).  DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults’ specific technological fears and practical barriers.
